factCards.short_description: Der Botanische Garten auf der Morgenstelle wurde 1968 eröffnet und gehört zur Forschung und Lehre der Universität Tübingen. Zugleich ist er ein Ort zum Spazieren und Schauen. Etwa zehntausend Pflanzenarten wachsen hier auf zehn Hektar. Draußen führen Wege durch unterschiedliche Gartenbereiche; in den Gewächshäusern stehen tropische Pflanzen. Jenseits des Nordrings liegt außerdem das Arboretum mit seltenen Bäumen. Wer hier geht, bewegt sich durch eine wissenschaftliche Sammlung lebender Pflanzen. Der Garten hat eine andere Aufgabe als ein reiner Stadtpark, auch wenn man in beiden eine Pause machen kann.

Die Gartenbereiche reichen von Pflanzenwelten der Alpen bis zu tropischen Beständen in den Gewächshäusern. Ein Gang durch das Freiland und der Blick in ein Gewächshaus zeigen deshalb unterschiedliche Teile derselben Sammlung. Jenseits des Nordrings liegt außerdem das Arboretum mit seinen seltenen Bäumen.

factCards.short_description: Die Schloss-Sternwarte gehört zu einer Geschichte präziser Winkelmessung: Johann von Bohnenberger erhielt 1818 den Auftrag, Württemberg zu vermessen. Den Nullpunkt legte er auf die Spitze des Nordostturms von Schloss Hohentübingen. Für sein Messinstrument hatte er bereits 1814 auf der Bastion ein kleines Observatorium mit drehbarer Kuppel bauen lassen. Dort entdeckte der Wissenschaftler Alfons Renz 2002 das originale Gerät wieder. Nach der Restaurierung kehrte der Reichenbach’sche Wiederholungskreis 2018 an seinen Aufstellungsort zurück. Er war Mathematiker und Astronom an der Universität Tübingen und legte den Nullpunkt seiner Messungen auf die Spitze des Nordostturms.

Unter der kleinen Kuppel auf der Bastion stand dagegen sein Messinstrument: der große Wiederholungskreis. Bohnenberger hatte dieses Observatorium bereits 1814 errichten lassen. Der Kreis gehörte zu den modernsten Winkelmessgeräten seiner Zeit. Die Kuppel ließ sich drehen. So erhielt das Instrument einen eigens für seine Arbeit gebauten Raum auf der Schlossbastion.

Nach Bohnenbergers Tod 1831 geriet die kleine Sternwarte in Vergessenheit. Fast zwei Jahrhunderte nach ihrem Bau fand der Tübinger Wissenschaftler Alfons Renz dort 2002 das Originalgerät wieder. Das war mehr als die Wiederentdeckung eines historischen Gebäudes: Auch der nahezu vollständige Wiederholungskreis war an seinem ursprünglichen Aufstellungsort erhalten geblieben.

Das Landesamt für Denkmalpflege restaurierte das Gerät. Währenddessen wurde auch das Observatorium saniert. 2018 kehrte der Reichenbach’sche Wiederholungskreis zurück, zum zweihundertjährigen Jubiläum des Beginns der württembergischen Landesvermessung.

Vom Schloss aus ging es bei dieser Arbeit weit über den Schlossberg hinaus: Bohnenbergers Auftrag galt dem ganzen Königreich. Die kleine Kuppel auf der Bastion und der Bezugspunkt oben am Turm gehören zu diesem gemeinsamen Vorhaben.

factCards.title: Schlosslabor: DNA aus gebrauchten Verbänden
factCards.short_description: Im Schlosslabor von Hohentübingen entdeckte Friedrich Miescher 1869 die Substanz, die wir heute DNA nennen. Sein Ausgangsmaterial waren benutzte Wundverbände aus dem Tübinger Krankenhaus. Aus dem Eiter gewann er weiße Blutkörperchen und untersuchte ihre Zellkerne. Den unbekannten Stoff nannte er Nuklein. Welche Bedeutung er für die Vererbung hatte, konnte Miescher damals noch nicht wissen. Sein Lehrer Felix Hoppe-Seyler prüfte die Ergebnisse zunächst selbst; veröffentlicht wurden sie erst 1871. Die Entdeckung begann also in einer umgebauten Schlossküche, mit unappetitlichem Material und einer sorgfältigen Prüfung statt sofortiger Gewissheit.
factCards.deep_dive_text:
Im Schlosslabor von Hohentübingen begann Friedrich Miescher im Herbst 1868, weiße Blutkörperchen zu untersuchen. Die Universität hatte die frühere Schlossküche bereits 1818 zum chemischen Labor gemacht. Hier arbeiteten Forscher an den chemischen Vorgängen in Lebewesen. Felix Hoppe-Seyler, seit 1861 Professor in Tübingen, untersuchte den roten Blutfarbstoff und gab ihm den Namen Hämoglobin.

Miescher brauchte viele Zellen für seine Versuche. Er sammelte gebrauchte Wundverbände im Krankenhaus und wusch die weißen Blutkörperchen aus dem Eiter. Anfang 1869 fand er in den Zellkernen eine bisher unbekannte Substanz. Er nannte sie Nuklein, nach dem lateinischen Wort für Kern. Um sie genauer zu untersuchen, setzte er Pepsin aus Schweinemägen ein. Das Enzym zersetzte die Proteine, sodass die Kernsubstanz isoliert werden konnte.

Die Analyse zeigte einen hohen Phosphoranteil. Die Rolle des Stoffes als Träger der Erbinformation blieb Miescher jedoch unbekannt. Auch sein Lehrer nahm das Ergebnis nicht einfach hin: Hoppe-Seyler überprüfte die Experimente. Erst 1871 erschien Mieschers Arbeit.

Im Museum ist ein originales Präparat aus Mieschers Hand erhalten. Es stammt wahrscheinlich aus der Zeit um 1871, als er in Basel mit Rheinlachsen weiterforschte. Die Aufschrift lautet „Nuclein aus Lachssperma / F. Miescher“. Miescher hatte inzwischen anderes Ausgangsmaterial gewählt. Das kleine Gefäß gehört damit zur Fortsetzung jener Arbeit, die in Tübingen mit gebrauchten Verbänden begonnen hatte.

factCards.title: Spital: Fürsorge und ein Platz fürs Alter
factCards.short_description: Das Tübinger Spital war eine soziale Einrichtung für sehr unterschiedliche Menschen: Arme, Kranke, Reisende und Findelkinder sollten hier Hilfe erhalten. Die Pfalzgrafen gründeten es um 1260/70. Im Spätmittelalter verschob sich der Schwerpunkt. Wohlhabende Bürger konnten sich als Pfründner einkaufen und ihre Versorgung im Alter sichern. Der langgestreckte, verputzte Fachwerkbau stammt aus dem frühen sechzehnten Jahrhundert. Hinter ihm liegen weitere Gebäude um einen Hof. Diese Anlage erzählt deshalb zugleich von öffentlicher Fürsorge und von einer Altersversorgung, zu der Vermögen den Zugang eröffnete.
factCards.deep_dive_text:
Das Spital in der Tübinger Altstadt war ursprünglich für eine breite soziale Aufgabe gedacht. Arme sollten aufgenommen, Hungernde und Dürstende versorgt werden. Reisende brauchten Unterkunft, Kranke Betreuung; arme Frauen sollten bei der Geburt Hilfe erhalten und Findelkinder aufgezogen werden. Diese Aufgabenbeschreibung stammt aus der Gründungszeit im dreizehnten Jahrhundert. Die Tübinger Pfalzgrafen gründeten die Einrichtung um 1260/70.

Der heute sichtbare langgestreckte, zweigeschossige Bau ist jünger. Er stammt aus dem frühen sechzehnten Jahrhundert und besteht aus verputztem Fachwerk. Zusammen mit den Gebäuden hinter ihm bildet er eine Anlage um einen Innenhof. Zum Spital gehörten auch Scheunen, Stallungen und Wirtschaftsgebäude. Das Ensemble war also umfangreicher als das Haus, das man von der Straße wahrnimmt.

Im Spätmittelalter veränderte sich der Charakter der Einrichtung. Wohlhabende Stadtbürger kauften sich als sogenannte Pfründner ein. Dafür erhielten sie Versorgung und Pflege im Alter. Aus dem umfassenden Anspruch der Armenfürsorge entwickelte sich damit eine Versorgungsanstalt für Menschen, die einen solchen Platz bezahlen konnten.

Im Spital befindet sich das Altenzentrum Bürgerheim. Der Ort hat die Versorgung älterer Menschen damit als eine seiner Aufgaben behalten. An der Gebäudestruktur um den Hof lässt sich noch erkennen, dass hier eine größere städtische Einrichtung und kein einzelnes privates Wohnhaus stand.

factCards.title: Kornhaus: erst Getreide, dann Stadtgeschichte
factCards.short_description: Das Kornhaus beherbergt seit 1991 das Tübinger Stadtmuseum, wurde aber für ganz andere Aufgaben gebaut. Unten lagerte und handelte man Getreide, oben trafen sich Bürger zu geselligen Veranstaltungen. Später kamen Schulkinder, dann Feuerwehr und Rotes Kreuz ins Haus. Heute gehört Lotte Reiniger zu den Themen des Museums. Die Trickfilmpionierin schuf seit den zwanziger Jahren Filme mit Scherenschnitten. Zwischen dem alten Wirtschaftsgebäude und ihrer filigranen Filmtechnik liegt ein deutlicher Maßstabswechsel: Das Haus erzählt Tübinger Geschichte sowohl durch seine eigene Nutzung als auch durch die Menschen, deren Arbeit es zeigt.
factCards.deep_dive_text:
Das Stadtmuseum im Kornhaus nutzt ein Gebäude, das über Jahrhunderte Aufgaben für die Stadt übernommen hat. Der westliche Teil entstand 1453, der östliche etwa fünfzig Jahre später. Schon zuvor hatte an dieser Stelle ein Bau gestanden, der bei einem Stadtbrand zerstört wurde. Das Kornhaus gehört zu Tübingens alten Nutzbauten in alemannischer Fachwerkbauweise.

Im unteren Geschoss fand Getreidehandel statt. Die Räume darüber dienten bereits im siebzehnten Jahrhundert als Bürgerhaus für Tanz und gesellschaftliche Veranstaltungen. Reisende Komödianten spielten hier auch Theater. 1604 war das Haus um ein Geschoss aufgestockt worden.

Im neunzehnten Jahrhundert zog eine Volksschule ein. Sie wurde von Kindern der Weingärtner und Handwerker aus der Unterstadt besucht. Ab 1892 nutzten Feuerwehr und Rotes Kreuz das Kornhaus. Zwischen 1985 und 1991 wurde es zum Stadtmuseum umgebaut.

Zur Museumsarbeit gehört eine Ausstellung über Lotte Reiniger, die seit den zwanziger Jahren mit Scherenschnittfilmen arbeitete. Ihre Figuren gehören zu einer anderen Art von Handwerk als das Fachwerk des Hauses, doch beides lenkt den Blick auf gemachte Formen. Neben solchen künstlerischen Themen behandelt das Museum auch Stadtgeschichte und aktuelle Fragen. Für einen Gang durch das Kornhaus ist seine eigene Nutzungsgeschichte ein guter Anfang: Markt, gesellschaftlicher Treffpunkt, Schule und schließlich Museum haben nacheinander dieselben Räume gebraucht.

factCards.title: Sternwarte: Carl Boschs Fernrohr in Tübingen
factCards.short_description: Die Sternwarte auf der Waldhäuser Höhe nutzt ein Fernrohr mit einer Vorgeschichte in Heidelberg. Der Zeiss-Refraktor wurde 1925 gebaut und diente viele Jahre dem Nobelpreisträger Carl Bosch. Seit 1956 wird mit dem Instrument in Tübingen der Nachthimmel beobachtet. Sein Objektiv hat dreißig Zentimeter Durchmesser, seine Brennweite beträgt fünf Meter. Die astronomische Lehre der Universität reicht noch weiter zurück: Johannes Stöffler wurde 1507 als erster Astronomielehrer berufen. Das Fernrohr gehört also zu einer langen lokalen Tradition, kam aber als bereits benutztes Instrument aus einer anderen Stadt hierher.
factCards.deep_dive_text:
Die Sternwarte Tübingen auf der Waldhäuser Höhe verbindet öffentliche Himmelsbeobachtung mit der Geschichte eines älteren Instruments. Ihr Zeiss-Refraktor wurde 1925 konstruiert. Bevor er nach Tübingen kam, diente er viele Jahre Carl Bosch in Heidelberg als Beobachtungsfernrohr.

Seit 1956 wird mit diesem Gerät in Tübingen beobachtet. Dreißig Zentimeter beträgt der Durchmesser des Objektivs, fünf Meter die Brennweite. Diese Angaben beschreiben ein konkretes erhaltenes Instrument und keine bloße Erinnerung an frühere Astronomen.

Die universitäre Vorgeschichte beginnt wesentlich früher. 1507 wurde Johannes Stöffler als erster Lehrer für Astronomie an die Artistenfakultät der Universität berufen. Zwischen dieser frühen Lehre und dem Zeiss-Fernrohr liegen Jahrhunderte.

Die Astronomische Vereinigung gestaltet an der Sternwarte Vorträge und Beobachtungsangebote. Ob tatsächlich durch ein Fernrohr geschaut werden kann, hängt auch vom Wetter ab. Der Himmel gehört hier zum Programm, lässt sich aber nicht nach einem Veranstaltungskalender bestellen.

factCards.title: Ugge Bärtle: die Werkstatt hinter den Stadtfiguren
factCards.short_description: Das Ugge-Bärtle-Haus in der Herrenberger Straße führt zu dem Bildhauer zurück, dessen Arbeiten an mehreren Tübinger Plätzen stehen. Eugen Bärtle, genannt Ugge, bearbeitete Stein mit Spitzeisen und Hammer. Nach Ausbildung und Jahren in München und Hamburg kehrte er 1949 nach Tübingen zurück. Er gründete hier die Künstlervereinigung Ellipse und gehörte später zu den Initiatoren des Tübinger Künstlerbunds. Sein Atelier und der Skulpturengarten blieben weitgehend erhalten. Wer draußen seinen Weingärtner oder den Löwen am Technischen Rathaus gesehen hat, begegnet hier dem Arbeitsort hinter solchen öffentlichen Figuren.
factCards.deep_dive_text:
Das Ugge-Bärtle-Haus in der Herrenberger Straße 12 war Werkstatt und Wohnort des Tübinger Bildhauers Eugen Bärtle, genannt Ugge. Mit Spitzeisen und Hammer arbeitete er seine Skulpturen aus dem Stein. Der erhaltene Atelierbereich und der Skulpturengarten führen zu dieser handwerklichen Seite seiner Arbeit.

Bärtle lernte zunächst das Steinmetzhandwerk in Tübingen. Es folgten ein Studium an der Kunstakademie in München und weitere Jahre in Hamburg. 1949 kehrte er in seine Heimatstadt zurück. In der Nachkriegszeit gründete er die Künstlervereinigung Ellipse, die von 1951 bis 1965 bestand. 1971 initiierte er mit anderen den Tübinger Künstlerbund. Er arbeitete damit auch an Zusammenschlüssen, in denen Künstler der Stadt gemeinsam auftreten konnten.

Zwei seiner öffentlichen Figuren zeigen, wie verschieden seine Aufgaben waren. Der Weingärtner aus Muschelkalk von 1961 steht in der Salzstadelgasse und war ursprünglich eine Brunnenskulptur an der Krummen Brücke. Die Stadt wollte den Weingärtnern damit ein Denkmal setzen. Der Löwe von 1954 vor dem Technischen Rathaus wurde aus Granit geschlagen und als Wächterfigur für den Eingang entworfen.

Im Atelier beginnt der Blick auf diese Werke früher: beim Stein und dem Ort seiner Bearbeitung. Die Räume und der Garten wurden nach Bärtles Tod öffentlich zugänglich gemacht und blieben weitgehend in ihrem ursprünglichen Zustand.

factCards.title: Zoologische Sammlung: Tiere nach Herkunft geordnet
factCards.short_description: Die Zoologische Schausammlung der Universität Tübingen verteilt Tierpräparate auf zwei Ebenen. Oben stehen Tiere Mitteleuropas im Mittelpunkt, unten Tiere aus anderen Erdteilen, geordnet nach ihrer geografischen Herkunft. Manche Präparate sind mehr als hundert Jahre alt. Einige kamen als Geschenke des württembergischen Königshauses in die Sammlung, dessen Mitglieder Tiere von ihren Exkursionen mitbrachten. Neben Vögeln und anderen Wirbeltieren gibt es Insekten, Schnecken und Muscheln. Die Sammlung zeigt damit auch eine Art, Natur zu ordnen: nach Tiergruppen, nach Herkunft und nach den Beständen, die über lange Zeit zusammengetragen wurden.
factCards.deep_dive_text:
Die Zoologische Schausammlung der Universität Tübingen ist auf zwei Ausstellungsebenen verteilt. Der obere Saal heißt „Tiere der Heimat“ und konzentriert sich auf Mitteleuropa. Von den mehr als dreihundert heimischen Vogelarten sind dort nahezu alle vertreten. Hinzu kommen zahlreiche weitere Wirbeltiere und Insektengruppen, die sich mit bloßem Auge gut erkennen lassen.

Andere Teile richten den Blick auf Lebensräume und Spuren von Tieren. Gezeigt werden Forstschädlinge mit ihren Fraßbildern sowie Fische, die im Neckar leben oder früher dort vorkamen. Ein Fraßbild lenkt die Aufmerksamkeit vom Tierkörper auf die Wirkung seiner Tätigkeit. Beim Neckar steht dagegen ein bestimmter Fluss mit seiner Tierwelt im Mittelpunkt.

Im Erdgeschoss sind die Präparate nach geografischer Herkunft geordnet. Australien, Afrika, Asien und Amerika werden durch ausgewählte Tiere vertreten. Die ältesten Präparate sind über hundert Jahre alt. Einige wurden vom württembergischen Königshaus geschenkt; dessen Mitglieder hatten Tiere von Exkursionen mitgebracht. Die Sammlung besitzt deshalb neben ihrer zoologischen auch eine Sammlungsgeschichte.

Schnecken und Muscheln aus der Region und aus anderen Teilen der Welt ergänzen die Schau. Beim Gang durch die beiden Ebenen wechseln die Ordnungen: erst vertraute Tiergruppen und Lebensräume, dann die Herkunft aus verschiedenen Erdteilen. An diesen Entscheidungen lässt sich erkennen, wie eine Universität ihre zusammengetragenen Bestände für Betrachtung und Vergleich zugänglich macht.

factCards.title: Alte Aula: lecture rooms beneath a grain store
factCards.short_description: The Alte Aula on Münzgasse was once Tübingen University’s main building. Grain stored under its roof formed part of professors’ pay. The same house contained lecture rooms, a library and an archive; its senate awarded degrees and imposed penalties. Even the entrance tells you something about the site: from Münzgasse, you enter the five-storey building on the third floor because it stands on a steep south-facing slope. The crossed sceptres in the balcony railing belong to the university’s coat of arms. They recall an institution entitled to exercise jurisdiction over its own members.
factCards.deep_dive_text:
The Alte Aula brought together functions that would rarely fit into one university building today. It was probably built in 1547 on the site of earlier structures. Its predecessor, the “Sapienz”, had burned down a few years before. The new building was initially called “aula nova”. Its present name reflects the later relocation of the university’s centre.

Inside were the library, archive and lecture rooms, with a ceremonial hall and senate meeting rooms above. The attic stored grain because professors received part of their pay in agricultural produce. The university administered scholarly work, material supplies and its own jurisdiction in the same house. The crossed sceptres on the balcony refer to that separate legal status.

For the university’s 300th anniversary in 1777, the building acquired a hipped roof, rendered façades and a classical balcony. The alterations did not necessarily make the lecture rooms comfortable. An account from 1822 complains of darkness and cold, describing students bringing their own candle stubs.

In 1845, the Neue Aula on Wilhelmstraße replaced it as the main university building. After lengthy renovation, the Alte Aula became fully accessible again in 2012. Work uncovered a ceiling with paintings from 1547. The education library also returned from temporary premises. The building remained a university workplace despite losing its former central role.

factCards.title: Alter Botanischer Garten: the park that remained
factCards.short_description: The Alter Botanischer Garten between the old town and Wilhelmsvorstadt once belonged to the university’s scientific facilities. A botanical garden was established here in 1805 and moved to the Morgenstelle in 1969. The large trees remained within a public park often called “Bota”. The palm house did not survive. Built from glass and iron in 1886, it was demolished in 1970 despite a citizens’ campaign to save it. An initiative to rebuild it in 2009 also failed. Today’s park recalls both surviving greenery and a university building that has disappeared.
factCards.deep_dive_text:
Before the Alter Botanischer Garten housed the university’s plants, the site was already used for teaching and exercise. In the 17th century it served the physical training of students at the Collegium illustre. At various times, a riding hall and theatre stood here. The later garden therefore had an earlier life as a place for student exercises.

The university established its botanical garden in 1805, with an arboretum and greenhouses. The glass-and-iron palm house was built in 1886. When the botanical garden moved close to the new natural science institutes on the Morgenstelle in 1969, the old site lost its previous function. The palm house was demolished in 1970. A citizens’ campaign failed to prevent demolition, and an initiative in 2009 did not result in reconstruction.

The park also contains “Genius des Ruhms”, a marble monument dedicated to Hölderlin, made by Adrian Emmerich Andresen in 1872. The figure represents a genius, a protective spirit from Roman mythology, rather than a portrait of the poet. The sculpture was initially offered to the town for Hölderlin’s grave. Negotiations led instead to its placement in the garden in 1881.

Today the old garden is used as an urban park with a playground. Its scientific role moved elsewhere, while trees and artworks remained at the former site.

factCards.title: Pfleghof: the monastery’s business in town
factCards.short_description: The Bebenhäuser Pfleghof on Schulberg was the town office of Bebenhausen monastery. The monastery collected dues and income while itself being exempt from municipal charges. Its business took physical form here: produce was stored under the roof, and three large wine presses stood in the open hall. The complex was built between 1477 and 1502. Today it houses the musicology institute, and the former chapel is a rehearsal room. Its doorway still bears the Cistercian arms and the inscription “Soli deo 1492”. Religious and economic functions shared the same premises.
factCards.deep_dive_text:
The Bebenhäuser Pfleghof was not a second monastery inside the town. It was the place where nearby Bebenhausen monastery conducted business with Tübingen and its inhabitants. Bebenhausen was the town’s largest landowner and collector of taxes and dues, while itself exempt from municipal charges. The Pfleghof gave those property interests a substantial physical presence.

The three-wing complex was built between 1477 and 1502. Its courtyard helps explain the earlier use. An open ground-floor hall had large pointed-arch entrances and contained three wine presses. Storage spaces above held agricultural produce, raised into the building with a hoisting wheel and rope. The separate house above the complex served as the abbot’s town residence.

Towards Holzmarkt is the chapel doorway, bearing the Cistercian arms and the inscription “Soli deo 1492”. Beside it, Mary appears as the order’s patron. These religious signs belonged to a building used for storage, administration and winemaking.

New uses have changed the rooms. The former winepress hall is now a hall of the musicology institute, and the chapel serves as a music rehearsal room. The building also contains a musical instrument collection and student accommodation. The large pointed-arch entrances in the courtyard still show how open the original hall was. The abbots’ house stands above it as a separate building.

factCards.title: Burse: from introductory studies to hospital wards
factCards.short_description: The Burse on Bursagasse began as a residence and teaching building for the young university. Students learned the liberal arts here before progressing to medicine, law or theology. Early in the 19th century, its purpose changed dramatically: Johann Ferdinand Autenrieth converted it into a university clinic with 12 patient rooms. Friedrich Hölderlin was admitted in 1806 and discharged after 231 days, declared incurable. His treatment took place in the Burse, not the Hölderlinturm. The Zimmer family took him into the tower afterwards. Since 1971, humanities departments have occupied the Burse again.
factCards.deep_dive_text:
The Burse was built between 1478 and 1482 for the newly founded university’s arts faculty. Its “Artisten” were students of the liberal arts, not performing artists. They studied grammar, logic and rhetoric alongside arithmetic, geometry, astronomy and music. A master’s qualification gave access to the higher faculties of medicine, law and theology.

Philipp Melanchthon stayed as a teacher after completing his own master’s degree and left for Wittenberg in 1518. Johannes Reuchlin and Wilhelm Schickard are also among the teachers associated with the building. The Burse provided foundational academic training; it was not merely a general student residence.

Between 1803 and 1805, Johann Ferdinand Autenrieth converted it into the first university clinic. Hölderlin was admitted on 15 September 1806. Treatment lasted 231 days, and he was discharged on 3 May 1807, considered incurable at the time. The Zimmer family then took him into the nearby tower.

Outside the Burse, Johannes Kares’s bronze sculpture “Für Lotte”, made in 2011, commemorates Lotte Zimmer. She cared for Hölderlin in the nearby tower until his death in 1843. The names Lotte and Hölderlin are engraved in the bronze. Since 1971, the Burse has housed the university’s philosophy and art history departments.

factCards.title: Cotta-Haus: Goethe’s publisher on Münzgasse
factCards.short_description: The Cotta-Haus on Münzgasse housed a publishing business that distributed books by Goethe and Schiller. Johann Friedrich von Cotta took over the family firm in 1787 and developed it through close relationships with his authors. Goethe stayed with him for several days in September 1797 while travelling to Switzerland. A plaque commemorates that visit. The famous sign “Hier kotzte Goethe”, meaning “Goethe vomited here”, is on the neighbouring building. The official walking guide calls it a humorous inscription. Behind the joke is Goethe’s documented stay with his own publisher, a few steps from the Stiftskirche.
factCards.deep_dive_text:
The Cotta-Haus on Münzgasse had a publishing history long before Goethe’s visit. The Cotta’sche Verlagsbuchhandlung was founded in 1659. The business prospered after Johann Friedrich von Cotta took over the family firm in 1787. Cotta combined publishing skills with close personal relationships with his authors.

Alongside Goethe and Schiller, its authors included Wieland, Herder, Hölderlin, Tieck, Kleist and Jean Paul. The Humboldts and Schlegels also joined the list, followed by the Tübingen Romantics Uhland, Kerner and Schwab. Münzgasse was a working address in the book trade and the circulation of literature, rather than simply the location of a famous visit.

In September 1797, Goethe stopped here on his journey to Switzerland. He stayed in the southeast room on the first floor and described the narrow view between the Alte Aula and Stiftskirche into the Neckar valley. A plaque on the house commemorates the stay. On the neighbouring building, the sign “Hier kotzte Goethe” turns the famous visit into a joke.

The façade has its own history. The house probably received its Baroque painting around 1725; renovation in 1987 made it visible again. The decoration therefore predates both Cotta’s takeover and Goethe’s stay. The building, the publishing business and the commemoration of the visit belong to different periods in the same house’s history.

factCards.title: Evangelisches Stift: an education with board and lodging
factCards.short_description: The Evangelisches Stift on Klosterberg trained future Protestant ministers. In 1536, Duke Ulrich established a scholarship combining teaching, accommodation and meals. Later students included Johannes Kepler, Hegel, Schelling and Hölderlin, who became famous mainly outside the ministry intended for them. Hegel, Schelling and Hölderlin also embraced the ideas of the French Revolution and came into conflict with the institution’s strict rules. Access to this funded education was reserved for men for centuries. Women were first admitted to the Stift in 1969.

factCards.title: Fruchtkasten: grain, wine and the citizens’ office
factCards.short_description: The Fruchtkasten on Schmiedtorstraße was built in 1474 as a large agricultural store and working building. “Frucht” here refers chiefly to grain, kept beneath the multi-storey roof. Large wine presses occupied the ground-floor hall, which measures more than 28 metres long and 18 metres wide. The building later served as a school. After extensive restoration in 2003, the citizens’ office moved in and the rooms regained their open hall character. Behind today’s administrative desks is a building whose scale came from the demands of storing produce and making wine.
factCards.deep_dive_text:
The Fruchtkasten was a ducal storehouse dating from the late 15th century. According to the town walking guide, around 650 trees from the nearby Schönbuch were felled for its construction around 1474. Its Alemannic timber frame is oak. A building designed to hold substantial quantities of agricultural produce required a considerable amount of material.

Different floors had different uses. Grain was stored in the multi-storey roof space, and hops were added later. Large wine presses stood on the ground floor. The hall provided more than 28 metres in length and 18 metres in width, while another grape press occupied the cellar. Storage and processing took place beneath the same roof.

The building was renewed in 1770. It served as a school in the 20th century before extensive restoration in 2003. Since then, it has housed the citizens’ office, registry office, municipal treasury and other town services. Restoration returned the rooms to their earlier hall-like form.

Behind the Fruchtkasten, by the Fruchtschranne, a hand holding a small loaf recalls the neighbouring hospital and its provision for poor people. The emblem belongs to that institution’s history. A copy stands at the Fruchtschranne; the original is preserved in the Stadtmuseum. Storehouse, winepress and hospital emblem reveal different forms of provision within the same neighbourhood.

factCards.title: Hölderlin’s room and the Zimmer family
factCards.short_description: Friedrich Hölderlin lived in the Hölderlinturm beside the Neckar from 1807 to 1843, in the household of master carpenter Ernst Zimmer. A room on the first floor was his home for 36 years. The university clinic had previously discharged him after 231 days of treatment, declaring him incurable. Zimmer’s daughter Lotte also cared for him. The museum explores his life and his work with language. The familiar tower is a reconstruction, however: in 1875 the building burned down to its foundations.
factCards.deep_dive_text:
The Hölderlinturm preserves the memory of Friedrich Hölderlin, although the house had to be rebuilt after his death. A home was built here in the late 18th century on the base of an earlier defensive tower. After the fire of 1875, it was rebuilt in a historicist style with a pointed roof. By then, Hölderlin had already died.

His life in Tübingen began long before he joined the Zimmer household. From 1788 to 1793 he studied at the Evangelisches Stift, where Hegel and Schelling also lived during that period. He was writing poems while still a student, then worked as a private tutor and independent writer with support from Schiller. In 1806 he was admitted to the university clinic in the Burse. Ernst Zimmer took him into the nearby tower after that hospital stay.

Today’s exhibition occupies three floors. At its centre is Hölderlin’s table, his only surviving piece of furniture. The museum also treats language and rhythm as things visitors can work with themselves. A language laboratory offers opportunities to experiment with syllables, words and verse; a poetry trail continues into the garden.

The museum reopened in February 2020 after extensive renovation. The narrow Zwingel leads from the Neckarbrücke to the tower. Between the old town walls, Hölderlin’s home and his walking route were close together.

factCards.title: Holzmarkt: Hesse’s apprenticeship and public remembrance
factCards.short_description: Hermann Hesse learned the bookselling trade on the Holzmarkt. At Heckenhauer, in the red house at number 5, he began his apprenticeship in 1895 and later stayed on as an assistant. The square north of the Stiftskirche was also a place of trade: timber was sold here into the 20th century. Today many people associate it with the steps outside the church. It is also a place of remembrance. Plaques commemorate the persecution and murder of Tübingen’s Jews and the persecution of Sinti and Roma. Stolpersteine were added in 2018.
factCards.deep_dive_text:
The Holzmarkt takes its name from an actual trade. Timber was sold here into the 20th century. Earlier, the square also hosted the Hafenmarkt, where potters and coppersmiths offered their wares. The elongated square lies north of the Stiftskirche, and its fountain depicts Georg, one of the church’s patron saints.

The Georgsbrunnen figure dates back to 1523. Its design combines late Gothic forms with the early Renaissance. The figure in the square is a reproduction made by Eduard Raach-Döttinger in 1976; fragments of the original are in the Stadtmuseum. The date of the design and the age of the object on display are therefore different.

Opposite is Heckenhauer’s bookshop. Hesse served his apprenticeship there from 1895 to 1898 and remained for several months as an assistant. In 2013, the city opened the Hesse-Kabinett at his original workplace, with documents and reproductions concerning the writer’s life and work.

The wall above Neckargasse records a separate history. Memorial plaques commemorate the expulsion and murder of Tübingen’s Jews and the persecution of Sinti and Roma under National Socialism. Stolpersteine outside a clothing shop followed in 2018. While the church steps remain a gathering place, the plaques and Stolpersteine commemorate people expelled and murdered under Nazi rule.

factCards.title: Jakobuskirche: a building seam and a pilgrim saint
factCards.short_description: The Jakobuskirche on Jakobusplatz is Tübingen’s oldest surviving church. Its Romanesque nave dates from around 1200 and was later extended eastwards. An inscription on the outer choir wall records the start of construction: the first stone was laid on 10 June 1500. The seam between the building phases remains recognisable. Inside the choir, a vault keystone depicts Jakobus with a cloak, shell, staff and hat. The church stands on a feeder route towards Santiago de Compostela. Among the houses of the lower town, it belongs both to local building history and to the history of pilgrimage.
factCards.deep_dive_text:
The Jakobuskirche reveals different building periods within a relatively small structure. Its Romanesque nave dates from around 1200. A few small round-arched windows survive from that earlier fabric. The late Gothic choir extends eastwards, with a visible seam separating the building phases.

An inscription beneath a window on the outer choir wall gives 10 June 1500 as the date the first stone was laid. The present form therefore developed through an extension rather than a complete rebuilding at one moment. Inside are keystones, tomb monuments and epitaphs. There are also stone blocks carved with concentric circles. Their meaning remains uncertain.

Jakobus appears on a keystone in the choir vault, wearing a cloak and carrying the familiar pilgrim attributes of shell, staff and hat. The church stands on a feeder route to Santiago de Compostela. Pilgrimage may also have played a part in the church’s foundation.

Everyday life in the lower town continued around it. A pig market was held behind the church into the 1950s. The same square hosts a market on Saturday mornings today. Alongside worship and pilgrimage, the church’s history includes the business and animals of the surrounding neighbourhood.

factCards.title: Johanneskirche: after the ballroom church
factCards.short_description: The Johanneskirche on Froschgasse was built between 1875 and 1878 for the Catholic congregation. Its predecessor occupied an unusual space: in 1818, the former ballroom of the Collegium illustre had been converted into a parish church. The new building was Neo-Gothic and dedicated to the apostle and evangelist Johannes. Today it is also the university church of the Catholic theology faculty. Its musical life includes three choirs, a Rieger organ with over 40 stops and a small chamber organ. It recalls a congregation re-established after the Reformation, initially worshipping in a converted hall.
factCards.deep_dive_text:
The Johanneskirche belongs to the history of Catholic life in 19th-century Tübingen. Württemberg, elevated to a kingdom in 1806, had acquired Catholic territories. This changed the religious composition of the country. A Catholic theology faculty was established at Tübingen University in 1817. The town’s first Catholic parish since the Reformation developed in the following period.

At first, the congregation used the former ballroom of the Collegium illustre, converted into a church in 1818. The present Johanneskirche was built between 1875 and 1878 to replace that earlier church a little further south. Its Neo-Gothic architecture belongs to the 19th century, even though its forms look back to older church buildings.

The stained glass in the choir depicts the testimony of Johannes the Baptist, scenes from the life of Jesus and episodes involving the patron, Johannes the Evangelist. The musical equipment includes a Rieger organ with more than 40 stops and a chamber organ from Jürgen Kopp’s workshop in Aurich. Three choirs contribute to the church’s musical life.

Near the Johanneskirche and Wilhelmsstift is Wilhelm Pfeiffer’s bronze “Sitzende”, made in 1982, depicting a seated girl. Parts of the bronze patina are worn away, and flowers are placed between the figure’s arms. In its neighbourhood, the sculpture is touched and decorated as well as looked at.

factCards.title: Judengasse: a neighbourhood and an expulsion
factCards.short_description: Judengasse beside the Krumme Brücke recalls the medieval neighbourhood of Tübingen’s Jewish residents. It is first documented in 1398. When Count Eberhard im Barte founded the university in 1477, he also ordered the Jews expelled from the town. The foundation of the university coincided with the loss of home for part of its population. Little is known about earlier life in the lane. Basin-like wells in some cellars may have served as ritual baths, but that interpretation is uncertain. Even the street name was changed in 1943, before the old name returned in 1945.
factCards.deep_dive_text:
Judengasse identifies a specific place of medieval Jewish life in Tübingen. The first Jewish residents probably arrived in the 12th or 13th century. The lane’s name is securely documented in 1398. Some house foundations reach back to the 13th century. Basin-like wells surviving in cellars have been interpreted as possible ritual baths, although that use is not established.

In 1477, Count Eberhard im Barte ordered the Jewish population expelled from Tübingen. The university was founded in the same year. For the Jewish residents, that year meant being forced to leave their homes. Little is known today about their daily lives in the houses along the lane.

Jewish people began moving to Tübingen again from 1850. The synagogue built in 1882 stood on Gartenstraße, outside the old town, and belonged to this later community. After its destruction during the pogrom night, many fled into exile; those who remained were deported in 1941 and 1942.

The lane’s name was also changed under Nazi rule. In 1943 it became “Schotteistrasse”, after the “Schottei”, an establishment where National Socialists met. The old name returned in 1945. No Jewish residents were living in the lane during the Nazi period. Its name recalls the medieval neighbourhood, while the persecution of the later community also concerns other places in town.

factCards.title: Krumme Brücke: water for work and daily life
factCards.short_description: The Krumme Brücke crosses the Ammerkanal at the boundary between Tübingen’s upper and lower town. Water here was a working resource. Tanners processed hides on platforms over the canal, while dyers lived and worked in Ammergasse. The channel also carried wastewater away and supplied firefighting water. The small pond beside the bridge, the Wette, watered livestock and was used for washing horses. The bridge is recorded in 1398. Its name probably comes from the bend in the road and the curved timber structure that followed it. The waterway belonged to the daily life of a craft and winegrowing neighbourhood.
factCards.deep_dive_text:
The Krumme Brücke connects two differently shaped parts of the old town. It marks the boundary between the upper and lower town, and its first written mention dates to 1398. The name is usually explained by the curve of the road, which the earlier wooden bridge probably followed.

Beneath it runs the Ammerkanal. The channel had several purposes: it supported trades, drained water, carried waste away and supplied water for firefighting. Ammergasse contained the homes and workplaces of tanners and dyers. Platforms projected over the water in front of the houses, allowing hides to be worked there. The canal-side location was directly connected with these occupations.

The little pond beside the bridge was called the Wette. Livestock drank here, and horses and vehicles could be washed. The fire service also used the pond as a water reservoir. A livestock market took place in the nearby surroundings of the Jakobuskirche.

Beside the bridge stands the Bürgerheim, a long timber-framed building dating from the early 16th century. It has been used for social purposes, including as the municipal hospital. Today it offers different forms of care for older people. This small square brings former working infrastructure, agricultural life and a long history of care into close proximity.

factCards.title: Neptune and the people of the Marktplatz
factCards.short_description: Neptune stands above a fountain on Tübingen’s Marktplatz with a history reaching back to Bologna. Heinrich Schickhardt designed it after the fountain there; Georg Müller executed the work in 1617. Over the centuries, the original sandstone deteriorated. The present version dates to a reconstruction in 1948, funded almost entirely by donations from local residents. Profiles of people involved even appear in the decorative water pipes. Among the square’s tall houses stands a work of art that the people of Tübingen helped remake, long after its original creation.
factCards.deep_dive_text:
The Marktplatz first appears in written records in 1302, while traders in Tübingen are documented as early as 1191. Most of the tall houses around the square date from the 15th and 16th centuries. Trade continued here. The weekly market shares the square with gatherings around the fountain, especially on warm summer evenings.

Heinrich Schickhardt based the Neptunbrunnen on a fountain he had sketched in Bologna during a journey through Italy. The Stuttgart sculptor Georg Müller executed his design in 1617. Neptune carries his trident, while the female figures at his feet represent the four seasons. The Roman water god and the seasons thus found a shared place on Tübingen’s market square.

Fragments of the original sandstone survive in the Stadtmuseum. After the Second World War, the municipal administration, residents and the French military government worked together on the reconstruction. The 1948 version was the first municipal building project after the war devoted solely to artistic purposes. Residents’ donations paid almost all the cost. Profiles in the decorative water pipes commemorate participants.

Literary history also belongs to the square. Hermann Kurz lived until his death in the house now occupied by a café and restaurant. His daughter Isolde Kurz spent part of her youth there. This was a place of trade, a home and, later, a site of collective restoration.

Neptune carries his trident, while the female figures at his feet represent the four seasons. The Roman water god and the seasons thus found a shared place on Tübingen’s market square.

Fragments of the original sandstone survive in the Stadtmuseum. After the Second World War, the municipal administration, residents and the French military government worked together on the reconstruction. The 1948 version was the first municipal building project after the war devoted solely to artistic purposes. Residents’ donations paid almost all the cost. Profiles in the decorative water pipes commemorate participants.

Literary history also belongs to the square. Hermann Kurz lived until his death in the house now occupied by a café and restaurant. His daughter Isolde Kurz spent part of her youth there. This was a place of trade, a home and, later, a site of collective restoration.

factCards.title: Neckarfront: a university beside the river
factCards.short_description: Tübingen’s Neckarfront brings the buildings of the old university town into a single view. Looking upstream from the Neckarbrücke, the sequence includes the Stiftskirche, Hölderlinturm, Burse, Evangelisches Stift and Schloss Hohentübingen. These neighbouring buildings held very different places in Friedrich Hölderlin’s life. He studied at the Stift, later received treatment in the Burse after it became a clinic, and finally lived with the Zimmer family in the tower. Buildings that seem close together in the panorama belonged to separate chapters of his life. The riverfront offers a way into those histories as well as a view of old façades.
factCards.deep_dive_text:
The Neckarfront brings Tübingen’s defences, homes and university into close proximity. Houses were already being built on the riverside town wall in the Middle Ages. Beneath the familiar façades is part of an earlier defensive structure.

The university buildings did not always have the same purpose. The Burse was built between 1478 and 1482 to accommodate and teach students. Between 1803 and 1805 it became Tübingen’s first university clinic. It now houses philosophy and art history. In the nearby Alte Aula, the university once kept its library and archive alongside lecture rooms. Its senate also met there to award degrees and impose penalties on members of the university.

Higher up the hill, academic life moved into a former seat of political power. In 1816, King Wilhelm I. transferred the whole of Schloss Hohentübingen to the university. For a time the library occupied the knights’ hall; an observatory was installed in the northeast tower and a chemical laboratory in the castle kitchen.

The opposite bank and the Platanenallee offer views that bring these buildings together. Within this compact space, individual buildings repeatedly acquired new uses. A student residence became a clinic, a kitchen became a laboratory, and a castle became university premises. Those specific changes give the panorama its history.

factCards.title: Nonnenhaus: Leonhard Fuchs and his herb garden
factCards.short_description: The physician and botanist Leonhard Fuchs lived and worked at the Nonnenhaus. He moved in in 1535 and planted a garden beside it for his research into medicinal plants. His plant book appeared in 1542 with more than 500 woodcuts, followed by the German “New Kreüterbuch” in 1543. A marble book nearby now commemorates that work. The name Nonnenhaus comes from earlier residents, women engaged in charitable work in the 15th century. Another detail belongs to everyday history: the little “Sprachhaus” projecting over the lane was a privy directly above the Ammerkanal.
factCards.deep_dive_text:
The Nonnenhaus connects a women’s community with the work of a medical professor. In the 15th century, Beguines or recluses lived here, women who devoted themselves to charitable work. The timber-framed house takes its name from them. Only after the Reformation did the house become a medical professor’s home.

Fuchs moved in in 1535 after Duke Ulrich appointed him professor of medicine in Tübingen. Beside the house he planted a herb garden to study medicinal plants. It was Tübingen’s first botanical garden, planted beside the professor’s home. The small garden and stone book nearby commemorate that work.

In 1542, Fuchs published “de historia stirpium commentarii”, illustrated with more than 500 woodcuts. The German “New Kreüterbuch” followed in 1543. Fuchs also served seven times as rector of the university. Fuchsias, named after him, preserve his name beyond the history of medicine.

The marble “Kräuterbuch” beside the Nonnenhaus was made in 1981 by Wolfgang Kubach and Anna Maria Kubach-Wilmsen. The artists are known for their stone books, including a tribute to Gutenberg in Mainz. Another surviving feature explains earlier sanitation: the exterior staircase leads to the “Sprachhaus”, a projecting privy above the Ammerkanal. Research, domestic life and everyday infrastructure occupied the same site.

factCards.title: Neckarinsel: the avenue came before the island
factCards.short_description: The Platanenallee on Tübingen’s Neckarinsel is older than the island itself. Its plane trees were planted in 1828, when they were no more than one and a half metres tall. Only around 1910 did a flood and industrial channel south of the avenue turn the site into an island. The path runs from the Neckarbrücke to the Silcher-Denkmal. That monument needs a different historical context: built in 1941, it used the composer Friedrich Silcher for Nazi propaganda. The park combines an old avenue, later water engineering and monuments with distinct histories.
factCards.deep_dive_text:
On the Neckarinsel, landscape design and public remembrance occupy the same space. The plane trees were planted in 1828; the flood and industrial channel south of the avenue only created the island around 1910. The trees were already established when the shape of the riverbanks changed. At planting, they had been no more than one and a half metres tall.

The old trees also require continuing care. They are inspected regularly, and some are connected by supporting cables. The high groundwater level is identified as a source of strain. Maintaining this historic avenue requires continuing attention.

At its end stands the Silcher-Denkmal, dating from 1941. It used the composer and his songs for Nazi propaganda. Scenes from Friedrich Silcher’s song settings “Wer will unter die Soldaten?” and “Der gute Kamerad” surround the composer. The 5.70-metre sculpture is accompanied by an enclosure and a stage structure; the plans also envisaged a parade ground.

The Wildermuth-Denkmal near the Alleenbrücke has a different origin. Dedicated to writer Ottilie Wildermuth in 1887, its obelisk carries a bronze portrait relief. The dedication explicitly names German women as the donors. Wilhelm Rösch made the monument, with Wilhelm Pelargus responsible for the bronze casting. The dedication on its front records who made this public remembrance of the writer possible.

factCards.title: The Rathaus clock: more than the time
factCards.short_description: The clock on Tübingen’s Rathaus displays more than the time of day. Johannes Stöffler created the astronomical clock in 1511, with indicators for the sun, moon and the so-called dragon hand. Its original zodiac dial is now in the Stadtmuseum. The clock itself was moved into the decorative gable in 1849. The painted façade is also younger than the town hall, built in 1435: it received its present design for the university anniversary in 1877. The building combines several generations of changes to the town’s public face.
factCards.deep_dive_text:
The Rathaus on the Marktplatz combined administration, justice and trade. Its medieval ground floor contained the municipal salt store and a prison. Bakers and butchers sold their goods in an open arcade, while tanners used the large first-floor hall as a salesroom. The town court and council met above them. Everyday commerce and civic authority shared one building.

Johannes Stöffler’s astronomical clock was added in 1511. Its original dial, decorated with zodiac signs, is preserved in the Stadtmuseum. Following its relocation in 1849, the clock sits in the decorative gable. Beside the ordinary time display, the astronomical dial uses three hands to indicate the date, phases of the moon and certain celestial events.

The façade was redesigned in a Neo-Renaissance style in 1877 for the university’s 400th anniversary. One of the building’s figures is a Bacchantin on the southeast corner. This follower of Bacchus, the god of wine, refers to the former importance of winegrowing.

The interior has also been changed and partly recovered. Offices once replaced the historic ducal court hall. During renovation between 2012 and 2015, the room was restored. Its present wall decoration reconstructs a scheme from the 1920s, discovered when the office partitions came down. The historic-looking parts of the Rathaus do not all come from its original construction.

factCards.title: Schloss Hohentübingen: science in the castle kitchen
factCards.short_description: At Schloss Hohentübingen, a kitchen became a research laboratory. The university installed a chemical laboratory there in 1818. In 1869, Friedrich Miescher discovered a substance from cell nuclei that he called “Nuklein”. He did not yet know its role in carrying hereditary information. His research took place in a building with a very different past: Hohentübingen was recorded as a castle in 1078 and later rebuilt as a Renaissance complex. King Wilhelm I. transferred the whole castle to the university in 1816. A library, observatory and laboratory found space within the former residence.
factCards.deep_dive_text:
Schloss Hohentübingen connects the history of political rule with experimental science. The lords of Tübingen sold the castle and town to the counts of Württemberg in 1342. The present four-wing complex, with its round towers, is shaped by Renaissance rebuilding. After occupying individual rooms, the university received the entire castle in 1816. Rooms acquired new purposes: the knights’ hall housed a library for a time, and the northeast tower became an observatory.

A chemical laboratory opened in the former kitchen in 1818. Here Friedrich Miescher began studying white blood cells in autumn 1868. He obtained them from used wound dressings collected at the Tübingen hospital, washing the cells out of the pus. Early in 1869 he isolated an unknown substance from their nuclei. He used pepsin from pigs’ stomachs to break down proteins so that he could examine this “Nuklein” more closely.

Miescher identified a high phosphorus content. He did not yet understand what the substance meant for heredity. His teacher Felix Hoppe-Seyler checked the results himself, and publication followed only in 1871.

An original preparation made by Miescher is exhibited in the Schlosslabor today. It probably dates from around 1871 in Basel, where he continued his research using salmon. The glass is labelled “Nuclein aus Lachssperma / F. Miescher”. His work continued after the Tübingen discovery.

factCards.title: Stiftskirche: stained glass and ducal tombs
factCards.short_description: The Stiftskirche St. Georg on Holzmarkt combines late Gothic church art with the history of Württemberg’s ruling family. Its choir became a dynastic burial place and now contains 14 stone monuments to dukes and their relatives. The choir stalls originally placed here have moved into the side aisles. Among the church’s most valuable works are the stained-glass windows made in Peter Hemmel von Andlau’s Strasbourg workshop between 1476 and 1480. The building’s arrangement and uses have changed over time. Its works belong together, but they were not all commissioned for the same purpose or at the same date.
factCards.deep_dive_text:
The Stiftskirche St. Georg had a predecessor: a parish church is documented here in 1191. In 1477 it became a collegiate church in connection with the university’s foundation. The present late Gothic building replaced the Romanesque church in the late 15th century, at the instigation of Count Eberhard im Barte.

The furnishings reward attention to different parts of the interior. A Gothic rood screen divides areas of the church. Beneath it is the winged altarpiece by Hans Leonhard Schäufelein of Nördlingen, a pupil of Dürer. A decorated baptismal font and stone pulpit also belong to the surviving furnishings. The stained glass from Peter Hemmel von Andlau’s workshop was made between 1476 and 1480. Its strong colours later attracted Goethe’s attention.

The choir underwent a particularly clear change of use. It originally contained the canons’ stalls, which now stand in the side aisles. It became a burial place for Württemberg’s ruling family. The closely arranged tomb monuments were made between 1450 and 1616. They span several generations of sculptors and patrons.

The church remains a religious space. Services and concerts take precedence over sightseeing. The choir also provides access to the tower, with views over the old town and far into the surrounding countryside.

factCards.title: Stocherkähne: opening the boats to everyone
factCards.short_description: Tübingen’s Stocherkähne are part of life on the Neckar beside the old town. Being able to take a trip without owning a boat was not always a given. For a long time, boating was restricted to owners, especially student fraternities. In the 1980s, the Bürger- und Verkehrsverein began offering a Stocherkahn on request to anyone. An activity available to a limited circle became publicly bookable. Trips follow the Neckarfront past the Hölderlinturm, Burse and Evangelisches Stift. The main landing stage is on the riverbank beside the Hölderlinturm.
factCards.deep_dive_text:
Access is part of the history of the Stocherkähne on the Neckar. For a long time, only people who owned a boat were permitted to take one out. Student fraternities in particular had boats of their own. This was not yet a publicly bookable service.

The Bürger- und Verkehrsverein changed that in the 1980s by offering trips on request. This helps explain why boating here is associated both with student traditions and with tourism. Residents also enjoy the trips as a way to spend time on their river.

The landing stage beside the Hölderlinturm places the boats within the old town’s riverside setting. A trip from this bank can be combined with a walk through the Zwingel. From the water, the focus is on the buildings of the Neckarfront: the Stiftskirche, Hölderlinturm, Burse and Evangelisches Stift, with Schloss Hohentübingen above them.

factCards.title: Universitätskarzer: paintings against graffiti
factCards.short_description: In the Universitätskarzer at Münzgasse 20, Tübingen University imprisoned mainly disobedient students. Offences could include night-time disorder, gambling with dice or skipping sermons. Prisoners scribbled on the walls. In 1736, the university responded with an unusual commission: Gottfried Schreiber was to decorate the rooms with biblical and classical images and sayings. The university then exercised its own jurisdiction over its members. The prison was used from 1515 to 1845. Today it is closed to visitors because of substantial damage to its walls and ceilings.
factCards.deep_dive_text:
The Universitätskarzer on Münzgasse consists of two small barrel-vaulted rooms. From 1515 to 1845, it served as a prison for members of the university. The senate handled their legal cases, with the rector acting as chief judge. The university was therefore a separate legal community within the town.

These “cives academici” included more people than professors and students. Servants in professors’ households, craftspeople and printers could also hold the status. It brought privileges such as exemption from tolls and taxes. Most of those imprisoned in the Karzer were students, despite the university’s much wider legal community.

The listed offences range from secret marriage engagements and breaches of dress rules to drinking bouts, dice games and night-time disorder. Missing sermons could also bring punishment. University discipline therefore reached well into personal life.

Bored prisoners began scribbling on the walls. In 1736, the university commissioned Gottfried Schreiber to counter this with a decorative scheme. Biblical and classical images and sayings were intended to define the rooms. Those paintings are now part of the historic fabric that poses conservation difficulties. Serious damage to walls and ceilings led to the prison’s closure. The place survives, but its interior is not currently open for ordinary visits.

factCards.title: Unterstadt: the winegrowers’ quarter
factCards.short_description: Tübingen’s Unterstadt was the neighbourhood of winegrowers and craftspeople. Around the Jakobuskirche, its houses are smaller than those in the upper town, shaped more strongly by the university and civic elite. The difference in height was also a social distinction. Tanners and dyers worked beside the canal in Ammergasse, and livestock were traded by the Jakobuskirche. The name “Gôgenviertel” recalls the winegrowers, although the origin of “Gôg” is unknown. The sculpture “Wengerter” on Salzstadelgasse commemorates their occupation. It originally stood as a fountain figure at the Krumme Brücke.
factCards.deep_dive_text:
The Unterstadt is easier to understand through its former work than through the many jokes about the “Gôgen”. factCards.title: Wilhelmsstift: from aristocratic academy to seminary
factCards.short_description: Before becoming a Catholic study house, the Wilhelmsstift on Collegiumsgasse was an exclusive academy for Protestant noblemen’s sons. An inscription above its entrance promised education for nobles and “ander Leut”, other people. From 1596, those others were no longer admitted. Alongside politics and natural sciences, the curriculum included riding, fencing and dancing. The building gained a new purpose in 1817, when King Wilhelm I. established a seminary here. The name Wilhelmsstift belongs to that later phase. The Renaissance building itself dates from 1588 to 1592.
factCards.deep_dive_text:
Over the centuries, the Wilhelmsstift site has accommodated very different communities. A Franciscan monastery first occupied this location. It was dissolved in 1535 and burned down in 1540. The present building was constructed between 1588 and 1592 by master builder Georg Beer and his assistant Heinrich Schickhardt.

The institution was initially called the “Collegium illustre”. It was intended to train state officials and senior administrators. An inscription at the southeast entrance promises teaching for gentlemen of noble birth and other people; above it is the Württemberg coat of arms dated 1593. From 1596, admissions no longer matched that broad wording. The academy was reserved for Protestant noblemen’s sons, who came from across Europe.

Their curriculum combined academic knowledge with courtly skills. Politics, natural sciences and modern languages were taught alongside riding, fencing, dancing and tennis. The programme was designed around the social lives expected of its pupils.

In 1817, King Wilhelm I. established a Catholic seminary here. The university also received a Catholic theology faculty. These changes followed the expansion of the Kingdom of Württemberg to include Catholic territories. The former Protestant aristocratic academy became a residence and training institution for Catholic theologians. The surviving entrance inscription and the present name therefore belong to different educational systems that occupied the same building in succession.

factCards.title: Zwingel: a path between two walls
factCards.short_description: The Zwingel is the narrow path along the Neckarfront towards the Hölderlinturm. It occupies a strip between the inner town wall and a lower outer wall. Houses on the southern Neckargasse and Bursagasse still rest on the older wall, so the present walking route runs through part of the former defences. Near the Neckarbrücke, projecting stone blocks provide evidence of masonry dating to the 13th century. Today the Zwingelmauer is a place to sit overlooking the river. Hölderlin also enjoyed walking here, close to the house that later took his name.
factCards.deep_dive_text:
At the Zwingel, two lines of wall stand close together. The higher, older town wall supports houses on the southern Neckargasse and Bursagasse. In front of it was a lower outer wall, the Zwingermauer. Individual round towers reinforced this outer defence. The path occupies the former town ditch in the space between the walls.

Evidence of the fortification’s age survives near the Neckarbrücke. The projecting stone blocks there are associated with the Hohenstaufen period and date back to the 13th century. The Hölderlinturm beside the path is later: a house was built in the late 18th century on a projecting defensive tower base. The house and its base therefore belong to different building phases.

The space is no longer used for defence. A narrow path runs beside the water and the wall has become a meeting place, with views across the Neckar towards the Platanenallee. Hölderlin particularly enjoyed walking here, close to the tower where he lived.

factCards.title: How Tübingen's coffee cups reached Germany's highest court
factCards.short_description: Tübingen's town hall also has a story about takeaway coffee cups. Since the beginning of 2022, the city has taxed disposable food and drink packaging to discourage litter and encourage reusable containers. A McDonald's franchise operator challenged the rule. The dispute reached Germany's Federal Constitutional Court, which rejected the complaint in a decision published in January 2025. The city celebrated. McDonald's criticised the paperwork and the prospect of different rules in different towns. A local charge on disposable packaging had become a national question about what municipalities are allowed to tax.
factCards.deep_dive_text: Tübingen introduced its packaging tax on the first of January 2022. It applies to sellers supplying food and drink in disposable packaging, and also covers single-use tableware and cutlery. The idea was to give businesses a financial reason to use reusable alternatives. A McDonald's franchise operator challenged the regulation and initially won. In March 2022, Baden-Württemberg's Higher Administrative Court declared it invalid. One central issue was location: customers buying takeaway food can eat it outside the city. Could the charge still count as a local consumption tax? The Federal Administrative Court reached a different conclusion in May 2023, largely upholding the regulation. The subsequent constitutional complaint also failed. Germany's Federal Constitutional Court explained that the normal pattern of local consumption was what mattered. Exceptional cases did not invalidate that principle. The court also found the interference with sellers' occupational freedom constitutionally justified. Its decision was published on the twenty-second of January 2025. Mayor Boris Palmer welcomed the result as a success for environmental protection and municipal self-government. McDonald's argued that varying local rules made things confusing and increased administration. The judgment settled the constitutional challenge, rather than every practical objection. Whether this kind of tax works well is a separate question from whether a city has the legal power to introduce it.

factCards.title: Anlagenpark: travelling nymphs beside the lake
factCards.short_description: The Anlagenpark between the station and town centre combines its lake with play areas, seating steps and green paths. Beside the water stands a sculpture with a longer journey behind it. The Water and Meadow Nymphs were created in 1810 and moved from Stuttgart to Tübingen in 1926. The group outdoors is a cast-stone copy from 1986; the original is protected from the weather in the Kunsthalle. Between waiting for a bus and resting by the lake, you encounter a work whose location and material have changed over time.
factCards.deep_dive_text:
The Anlagenpark lies between the station and town centre. Its facilities belong to everyday urban life: a lakeside terrace, a water playground, seating, a pirate-themed playground and an exercise area. An inclusive café with two terraces connects the park with the bus station. Stopping here does not require a separate expedition out of town.

Some of the sculptures beside the lake have histories much older than these present-day uses. Johann Heinrich Dannecker’s Water and Meadow Nymphs date from 1810. The group originally stood in Stuttgart, between the north wing of the Neues Schloss and the Eckensee. It moved to Tübingen’s Anlagensee in 1926. The meadow nymph adorns the water nymph with a wreath of flowers.

The original, carved in Keuper sandstone, is kept in the Kunsthalle to protect it from the weather. A cast-stone replica made in 1986 stands beside the lake. The difference between original and copy is therefore part of this place’s history.

Another nymph, near the Mühlbachsteg, was carved in marble by Karl Merz in 1910. It originally stood as a fountain figure in a setting designed by Theodor Fischer outside the Neckarmüllerei. The park brings together art made for other locations, alongside its spaces for play and passing through.

factCards.title: Bebenhausen: monastery, royal home, parliament
factCards.short_description: At Bebenhausen, monks, monarchs and eventually a state parliament used the same extensive complex. Cistercians took over the monastery in 1190. After the Reformation it became a Protestant monastery school, and in the nineteenth century Württemberg’s kings turned ancillary buildings into a hunting palace. The last royal couple, Wilhelm II and Charlotte, lived here in exile from 1918. Between 1947 and 1952 Bebenhausen hosted the parliament of Württemberg-Hohenzollern. Beyond its medieval buildings lies a history of repeated adaptation to different ways of living together and governing.
factCards.deep_dive_text:
Bebenhausen Monastery and Palace tell a story of changing uses within one complex. Cistercian monks arrived from Schönau near Heidelberg in 1190 and developed a wealthy monastery. Its surviving Gothic buildings include the summer refectory of 1335 and the church’s distinctive crossing tower, built between 1407 and 1409.

The monastery was dissolved during the Reformation in 1535. Its buildings then housed a Protestant monastery school until 1806. During the nineteenth century, Württemberg’s royal family adapted ancillary buildings as a hunting palace. The last royal couple, Wilhelm II and Charlotte, moved here into exile in 1918. Wilhelm died in 1921; Charlotte remained until her death in 1946. A palace kitchen dating from 1915/16 belongs to the surviving fittings of this later period.

Another phase began in 1947. Until 1952, Bebenhausen was the seat of the parliament of Württemberg-Hohenzollern. Parliamentary work followed monastic and royal occupation.

The village beside the complex has its own history. In 1823, seventeen families established a civic municipality with royal approval. Bebenhausen became part of Tübingen in 1974, and the entire settlement received protection as a historic ensemble in 1975. Walking through it, consider the monastery and village together. The story extends beyond the monastery walls and continued long after the monks had gone.

factCards.title: BOXENSTOP: from a personal Volvo to a museum
factCards.short_description: The BOXENSTOP museum began with a car its future founder actually drove: a 1962 Volvo PV 544. In 1976, that vehicle became the starting point of a growing collection. More vehicles had arrived by the time the motor museum opened in 1985. Historic toys soon joined the displays. The collection includes racing and sports cars, motorcycles, bicycles and more than two thousand toys. Full-sized vehicles and small-scale counterparts meet under one roof. A private interest gradually grew into a museum.
factCards.deep_dive_text:
BOXENSTOP began with a Volvo PV 544, built in 1962. In 1976, its owner still drove the car himself. That starting point developed into a private vehicle collection, which had grown considerably by the motor museum’s opening in 1985.

Old toys were added soon afterwards. They changed the scale at which transport could be seen. Alongside vehicles built for roads or racing circuits came objects through which people recreated those worlds in miniature. The collection includes historic racing cars, sports cars and racing motorcycles, as well as scooters and bicycles. Its more than two thousand toys include model railways in different gauges, cars, aeroplanes and ships. Dolls and dolls’ houses extend the collection beyond transport.

The exhibition grew to around twelve hundred square metres. Old advertising posters and enamel signs form part of its setting, along with lamps and chandeliers. The machines are therefore surrounded by other examples of historical design rather than simply displayed in isolation.

The beginning with a personally driven Volvo gives the larger collection an individual starting point. Between that 1962 vehicle and the toys added later, visitors can follow a change of scale: full-sized technical objects beside small models that brought versions of their shapes into everyday life.

factCards.title: Erich Fromm: books, notes and a literary estate
factCards.short_description: At the Erich Fromm Institut Tübingen, familiar book titles lead into a personal working collection. Fromm wrote Haben oder Sein and Die Kunst des Liebens; the institute also preserves his library, handwritten notes and unpublished texts. The collection’s presence in Tübingen owes much to Rainer Funk, Fromm’s last assistant and literary executor, supported by the Karl Schlecht Stiftung. Photographs and audio and video recordings accompany the books. Here, the author can also be approached through materials that were never prepared as finished books for a broad readership.
factCards.deep_dive_text:
The Erich Fromm Institut Tübingen preserves material belonging to the author of Haben oder Sein and Die Kunst des Liebens. His personal library accompanies published works, notes and other documents. Across about a hundred square metres, the collection places completed texts beside traces of the work behind them.

Handwritten notes and unpublished writings offer a different approach from a printed book. Photographs, sound recordings and video add further material. Researchers use these holdings to study Fromm’s thought and work.

The connection with Tübingen developed through Rainer Funk, a psychoanalyst who was Fromm’s last assistant and the executor of his estate. Support from the Karl Schlecht Stiftung helped make the institute possible. The place is therefore linked to Fromm through the preservation and study of his papers. Personal books and unpublished texts reveal how much material survives beyond the familiar titles through which an author is usually encountered.

factCards.title: Scheunenfund: from high-wheeler to track bike
factCards.short_description: The Scheunenfund bicycle museum opened in 2011 in a listed barn in Weilheim. Friends had encouraged its founders to put their historic bicycles on public display. The oldest is an 1879 Starley & Hillman Ariel high-wheeler. A later period is represented by a motor-paced track bicycle used to win the Baden-Württemberg championship in 1983. Around a hundred square metres contain touring and sporting bicycles alongside children’s and riding-style bikes. A private collection became a small exhibition bringing together very different uses of the bicycle.
factCards.deep_dive_text:
The Scheunenfund bicycle museum occupies a listed barn in Weilheim. The private collection opened to the public in summer 2011, after friends encouraged its founders to display their historic bicycles across roughly a hundred square metres.

An 1879 Starley & Hillman Ariel high-wheeler is the collection’s oldest bicycle. One of the later exhibits is a motor-paced track bicycle used to win the Baden-Württemberg championship in 1983. The two represent different periods and uses, from the historic high-wheeler to competitive cycling.

Touring bikes, sports bikes, children’s bicycles and riding-style bicycles also belong to the display. The historic exhibits remain rideable. Their different forms reflect the different demands placed on a sports bicycle and one intended for a child. The old barn provides one exhibition setting for these varied bicycle forms.

factCards.title: Französisches Viertel: life after the barracks
factCards.short_description: The Französisches Viertel grew on former military land after French troops left in 1991/92. Tübingen used the site for a neighbourhood bringing homes, work, services and culture close together. Former military buildings were incorporated into residential blocks of three to five storeys. The concept prioritised walking, cycling and public transport and received the German Urban Development Award in 2001. Beside the Panzerhalle, a sculpture even depicts the neighbourhood’s ground plan. Twenty-six young people made it in 2004 under Jürgen Klugmann’s guidance, turning urban planning into a shared artistic project.
factCards.deep_dive_text:
The Französisches Viertel developed from a former military site. When French troops withdrew in 1991/92, Tübingen gained the opportunity to reuse substantial areas in the south of the city. The Französisches Viertel and Loretto-Areal developed on a combined site of about sixty hectares. That figure refers to both neighbourhoods together, not just the Französisches Viertel.

The plan aimed to keep everyday journeys short. Housing, work, services and culture were closely combined. Former military buildings became part of residential blocks with three to five storeys. Rather than building another settlement on undeveloped land, the city created a mixed neighbourhood on an already occupied site. Social diversity and priority for non-motorised and public transport formed part of the concept. The development received the German Urban Development Award in 2001.

An artwork beside the Panzerhalle makes the neighbourhood plan its subject. The Corten steel sculpture dates from 2004. Twenty-six young people worked on it under Jürgen Klugmann’s guidance, giving it the form of the neighbourhood’s ground plan. Their project was called “An artwork for the Südstadt”.

factCards.title: Unterjesingen: wine press, workshop and farmhouse
factCards.short_description: The Keltermuseum in Unterjesingen spreads everyday history across several buildings. These include a wine-press building from 1784, the Zeeb-Haus built in 1609 and a fully preserved wheelwright’s workshop. Tools from farming, winegrowing and traditional crafts show what a village needed and made. The museum site expanded from 1986 as its supporting association incorporated the neighbouring Zeeb-Haus. Household objects accompany the working tools. Winegrowing thus opens into a broader account of domestic life and the crafts that supported rural communities. The buildings themselves are part of that history.
factCards.deep_dive_text:
The Keltermuseum stands in Unterjesingen’s historic centre. Its account of rural life occupies several buildings: the old wine-press building of 1784, the Zeeb-Haus of 1609 and a separately preserved wheelwright’s workshop. Moving between them connects different settings for work and domestic life.

The collection includes agricultural tools, winegrowing equipment and objects associated with traditional crafts from around 1860 onwards. Wheelwrights, coopers and saddlers are represented. Household objects place everyday life at home alongside professional work.

The village museum’s site expanded from 1986. Its supporting association was able to include the Zeeb-Haus immediately beside the wine-press building, adding another historic structure to the exhibition setting. The dates therefore distinguish the age of the buildings from their later use as a museum. The wine press and farmhouse existed long before the present collection; now they help place its objects within the context of rural buildings.
