factCards.title: Kunsthalle: a museum of changing exhibitions
factCards.short_description: The Kunsthalle Tübingen presents changing exhibitions of twentieth- and twenty-first-century art. One exhibition may focus on a single artist; another may bring works from different periods together around a shared question. Private collections of modern and contemporary art also feature in its programme. For a visit, the particular exhibition matters more than expecting to find the same pictures every time. The Kunsthalle also uses participatory interpretation and activities across generations. Its current programme, rather than a permanent list of exhibits, determines what you can see.
factCards.deep_dive_text:
The Kunsthalle Tübingen works through changing exhibitions. Some focus on an individual artist of the twentieth or twenty-first century. Others begin with a question and bring together works from different periods to explore it.

The subjects include both artistic and social issues. Such arrangements invite comparisons that would look different in a display organised strictly by date. Presentations drawn from private collections of modern and contemporary art add another strand to the programme.

The institution also uses interactive interpretation and activities across generations. People with different levels of experience are encouraged to engage with the works. Changing exhibitions therefore go alongside different ways of looking at the art together and discussing it.

factCards.title: The centre of the state in the Käsenbach valley
factCards.short_description: The geographical centre of Baden-Württemberg lies in Tübingen’s Käsenbach valley, according to the state surveying authority. A tilted stone cone has marked it since 1986. Weighing three tonnes and carved from shell limestone, it stands in the Elysium, a small wood celebrated by Swabian Romantic poets. The stone circle represents the state, while the cone tilts by eleven and a half degrees. A calculated centre becomes a designed resting place here. For Baden-Württemberg’s fiftieth anniversary in 2002, Tübingen’s civic foundation redesigned the setting with benches and information panels.
factCards.deep_dive_text:
A sculpture in the Käsenbach valley marks the geographical centre of Baden-Württemberg. The state surveying authority identified this location in 1980. Six years later, a three-tonne stone cone was installed. Made from Swabian-Franconian shell limestone, it has a polished grey surface and a conspicuous tilt.

Its form was designed rather than simply placed as a survey marker. The stone circle symbolises the state. The cone leans by eleven and a half degrees, half the Earth’s tilt. The sculpture translates its geographical subject into a particular material and shape.

The little wood is called Elysium, after the dwelling place of the blessed. Swabian Romantic poets were already celebrating it around 1830. The later designation as the state’s centre therefore arrived at a place with an existing name and literary history. For the state’s fiftieth anniversary in 2002, Tübingen’s civic foundation redesigned the site and added benches and information panels.

A steep path past the cone leads towards the meadow by the Luise-Wetzel-Stift, designated a natural monument. Plantings of the botanical garden lie nearby. The stone can therefore be a stop on a longer walk through the valley, with a steep climb beyond the shaded wood.

factCards.title: Mathematics: models from Brill’s teaching collection
factCards.short_description: In Tübingen University’s permanent mathematics exhibition, abstract thought takes physical form. Many models were made in Munich between 1875 and 1884 under Alexander von Brill and Felix Klein. When Brill was appointed to Tübingen in 1884, he ensured that the university acquired a complete collection of his models. They remained available for teaching. Computer-generated images and an interactive geometry screen now accompany the historic objects. Built models and calculated images sit alongside each other as different means of making mathematical forms visible.
factCards.deep_dive_text:
Tübingen University’s permanent mathematics exhibition displays models that give spatial form to mathematical ideas. Many were created in Munich between 1875 and 1884 under the guidance of Alexander von Brill and Felix Klein.

Brill’s appointment to Tübingen in 1884 brought this work into a new teaching setting. He ensured that the university possessed a complete collection of his models. They were intended for lectures and remain available for that purpose. The objects therefore belong to the history of teaching as well as to the history of mathematical ideas.

Mathematics at Tübingen developed from the Mathematical-Physical Seminar founded in 1869. Portraits of influential members of the department accompany the models in the exhibition.

Newer visual techniques extend the display. Computer-generated images from the Tübingen Geometry Workshop offer views of mathematical research, while the Imaginary touchscreen allows interactive exploration of geometry. Between a physical model and a screen, the means of showing a form changes. Making an abstract relationship visible connects the two.

factCards.title: Mineralogy: Urach rocks beside meteorites
factCards.short_description: Tübingen University’s mineralogical collection began in 1919 with the creation of a chair in mineralogy and petrography. Its display places local rocks beside minerals, ores and meteorites from further afield. Samples from the Urach volcanic area are specifically represented. Across about two hundred square metres, different geological settings meet: regional rock, striking crystals and material that reached Earth as meteorites. The collection also supports teaching. An object that first catches the eye through colour or shape becomes material for closer geological examination.
factCards.deep_dive_text:
Tübingen University’s mineralogical collection began in 1919, when a chair in mineralogy and petrography was established. It combines display with teaching, bringing together minerals, rocks, ores and meteorites.

Across about two hundred square metres, specimens from many parts of the world sit alongside material representative of south-western Germany and the surroundings of Tübingen. Rocks from the Urach volcanic area give the collection a regional connection. Selected meteorites extend its range beyond terrestrial places of origin.

A crystal’s shape or a mineral’s colour may provide the first reason to look more closely. In a geoscientific teaching collection, those properties stand beside questions about how rocks formed. Moving between the Urach samples and the meteorites therefore brings very different histories of origin into the same building.

factCards.title: MUT Alte Kulturen: a horse carved in mammoth ivory
factCards.short_description: At the Museum Alte Kulturen in Schloss Hohentübingen, mammoth-ivory figures are among the best-known objects. Around forty thousand years ago, people on the Swabian Alb carved animals including horses, mammoths and cave lions. The Vogelherd horse is one surviving example. The associated caves became UNESCO World Heritage in 2017. Inside the castle, these small originals join other records of human craftsmanship, including an ancient Egyptian offering chamber and ancient sculpture. The exhibition brings together several university collections. Its starting points are tangible objects, carved or shaped and preserved across very different lengths of time.
factCards.deep_dive_text:
The Museum Alte Kulturen in Schloss Hohentübingen displays the university’s archaeological and cultural collections. The Vogelherd figures are particularly well known. Around forty thousand years ago, people carved animals from mammoth ivory, including wild horses, mammoths and cave lions. The Vogelherd horse is one of these surviving early artworks.

The objects come from Ice Age caves on the Swabian Alb. In 2017, UNESCO added six caves associated with this art to the World Heritage List. The castle displays original finds, meaning the worked objects themselves. A flute fragment made from griffon vulture bone also belongs to the display. Alongside representations of animals, there is therefore evidence of early music.

The exhibition extends beyond the Ice Age. Other objects include the Tübingen armed runner, an ancient Egyptian offering chamber and the ancient sculptures of the Glyptothek in the Knights’ Hall. Different materials and forms share one building without belonging to the same historical period.

The exhibition occupies two thousand square metres, with around four thousand six hundred objects from seven collections. These figures describe the museum’s scale, not a compulsory itinerary. One ivory animal can be a more manageable starting point: look at its shape before moving on to larger objects and later cultures.

factCards.title: Natursteinpark Rongen: stone for sale and study
factCards.short_description: The Natursteinpark Rongen in the Schindhau woodland combines a stone yard, an educational trail and art displays. Around forty thousand tonnes of natural stone occupy twenty hectares, sorted and stacked. The stones are for sale, but can also be viewed. A geological trail explains the formation, composition and uses of local rocks at twenty-nine stations. An art trail adds contemporary sculpture and historic pieces. Walking through the site changes the questions asked of the material: how it formed, how it can be used and what shape someone has given it.
factCards.deep_dive_text:
The Natursteinpark Rongen lies in the Schindhau woodland. Its holdings are far larger than a collection in display cases: around forty thousand tonnes of natural stone occupy twenty hectares, sorted, stacked and piled. They are sold commercially while also forming part of a site visitors can explore.

The geological trail has three sections and twenty-nine stations. Short explanations describe the formation, composition and uses of different local rocks. The material is interpreted among the stone stocks themselves.

The art trail takes another approach. Historic individual pieces appear beside contemporary sculpture. Elements of English garden ornament made from cast stone, often following historical models, add another strand. Natural stone and cast stone are different materials within the same site.

A visit therefore connects raw material with worked forms. The grounds remain a commercial stone park: an object used for observation can also be an item for sale.

factCards.title: Neue Aula: beyond the old town
factCards.short_description: The Neue Aula opened in 1845 as Tübingen University expanded beyond its cramped old town. The classical building contained a ceremonial hall and fourteen lecture rooms. The two fountains outside have a less continuous history. The city gave them to the university for its anniversary in 1877. They were removed in 1931, and the square was also used for National Socialist rallies. Newly cast versions, based on historical engravings, returned in 1999. Today, Geschwister-Scholl-Platz carries traces of both the university’s expansion and the ruptures that followed.
factCards.deep_dive_text:
The Neue Aula opened in 1845 at the centre of a new university district. Its story begins with a shortage of space. The university was growing, and its buildings in the old town could no longer accommodate that growth. Expansion took it into the Ammer valley. The new district was named Wilhelmsvorstadt after King Wilhelm I of Württemberg.

The three-storey classical building made the change in scale visible. It contained a large ceremonial hall and fourteen lecture rooms. This was intended as the centre of an entire university district rather than simply another teaching room. Standing outside, you are looking at one starting point of the university’s move beyond the old town.

The city presented the two fountains in 1877, for the university’s four-hundredth anniversary. They did not remain here continuously. Removed in 1931, they were absent when the square served as a gathering ground for National Socialist rallies. The fountains visible again today are therefore not untouched originals. An art foundry in Süßen recast them using historical copper engravings, and they were installed on today’s Geschwister-Scholl-Platz in 1999.

The distinction matters when looking at the ensemble. The building belongs to nineteenth-century university expansion; the fountains also tell a story of removal and reconstruction. The Faculty of Law occupies the Neue Aula’s rooms.

factCards.title: Botanical garden: a living university collection
factCards.short_description: The botanical garden on the Morgenstelle opened in 1968 as part of Tübingen University’s research and teaching. It is also a place for walking and looking. Around ten thousand plant species grow here across ten hectares. Paths run through different outdoor sections, while greenhouses contain tropical plants. An arboretum with rare trees lies beyond the Nordring. Walking here means moving through a scientific collection of living plants. The garden has a different purpose from an ordinary city park, even though both can offer a place to pause.
factCards.deep_dive_text:

The garden’s sections range from Alpine plant life to tropical collections in the greenhouses. A walk outdoors and a look inside a greenhouse therefore reveal different parts of the same collection. Beyond the Nordring lies the arboretum with its rare trees.

The land below the garden also belongs to a possible longer walk. In the Käsenbach valley, the Elysium contains the geographical centre of Baden-Württemberg. factCards.title: Palaeontology: fossils in historic display cases
factCards.short_description: Tübingen University’s palaeontological collection combines fossil research with exhibition rooms that still contain some display cases from 1903. The collection itself began in the early nineteenth century. Its holdings include finds from the Swabian Alb and its foothills, alongside prehistoric specimens from Brazil and Africa. More than three thousand specimens form the display. Some carry memorable names, such as Tübinger Einzahnsaurier or Schwäbischer Lindwurm. Behind the historic setting is a research and teaching collection: these objects are also preserved for scientific work and university education.
factCards.deep_dive_text:
Tübingen University’s palaeontological collection began in the early nineteenth century. Fossils from the Swabian Alb and its foothills supplied abundant material for investigation. The collection has continued to grow since its foundation, combining display, research and teaching.

Some fossils remain in cases dating from the opening of the exhibition rooms in 1903. These are two different historical moments: the collection already had a longer history, while parts of its surviving display furniture date from that later year. Looking into one of these cases means seeing an old find within a historic setting of its own.

The holdings extend beyond the region. The collection includes Tübinger Einzahnsaurier, Schwäbischer Lindwurm and Schwabens Medusenhaupt, alongside prehistoric specimens from Brazil and Africa. More than three thousand finds are displayed. Their places of origin reach well beyond the Alb, with which Tübingen’s fossil research is closely connected.

The explanations are bilingual. Historic furniture does not mean the scientific interpretation stopped developing in 1903. The fossils remain part of the university’s research and teaching. The old cabinets contain objects that still belong to the work of present-day science.

factCards.title: Kopf|Sachen: putting perception to the test
factCards.short_description: Tübingen University’s psychological collection explores perception in its exhibition Kopf|Sachen – Mind|Things. Historical instruments and tests appear alongside optical illusions and phenomena involving touch. What eyes or hands report must be processed by the mind, and first impressions can mislead. The exhibition also addresses intelligence and competence tests and the precision engineering of scientific instruments. It connects sensory experience with experimental equipment. Behind a psychological investigation lies a physical workplace: instruments had to be made before researchers could use them to examine perception.
factCards.deep_dive_text:
Tübingen University’s psychological collection displays historical instruments and tests in Kopf|Sachen – Mind|Things. Its subject is the relationship between sensory impressions and their processing in the mind. Optical illusions concern vision, while haptic phenomena concern touch.

Intelligence and competence tests extend the exhibition beyond individual senses. Historic experimental equipment, the precision engineering of instruments and the department’s history accompany these subjects.

A psychological experiment here involves more than a question and an answer. Its history includes the objects researchers used to investigate perception. Between an illusion and the equipment for examining it lies the work of making a fleeting impression accessible to an experiment.

factCards.title: Castle cellar: a barrel for eighty-four thousand litres
factCards.short_description: In the cellar of Schloss Hohentübingen stands a giant wine barrel commissioned by Duke Ulrich in 1549. It measures approximately six metres eighty in length and four metres seventy in height, with a capacity of around eighty-four thousand litres. Yet it was filled with wine only twice. The barrel brings together two very different scales: enormous capacity and few actual fillings. Beneath the castle’s university rooms survives an object commissioned during the time when Württemberg’s dukes were responsible for the site.
factCards.deep_dive_text:
The giant wine barrel in the cellar of Schloss Hohentübingen dates back to a commission from Duke Ulrich in 1549. It measures approximately six metres eighty in length and around four metres seventy in height. Its capacity is about eighty-four thousand litres. With those dimensions, the barrel itself occupies a substantial part of the cellar’s character.

It was filled with wine only twice. Enormous capacity therefore does not automatically imply continuous use. The surviving object belongs to the castle’s ducal history, while the university later took over its rooms. In 1816, King Wilhelm I transferred the entire castle to the university. Above the old barrel, princely rooms became university workplaces. In the cellar, the duke’s commission remained.

factCards.title: Schloss-Sternwarte: measuring Württemberg
factCards.short_description: The Schloss-Sternwarte belongs to a history of precise angle measurement. Johann von Bohnenberger was commissioned to survey Württemberg in 1818 and placed his reference point at the top of Schloss Hohentübingen’s north-east tower. For his measuring instrument, he had already built a small observatory with a rotating dome on the bastion in 1814. Researcher Alfons Renz rediscovered the original instrument there in 2002. After restoration, the Reichenbach repeating circle returned in 2018. The little dome thus also belongs to the history of maps used to measure and describe land.
factCards.deep_dive_text:
The Schloss-Sternwarte at Hohentübingen belongs to the history of surveying Württemberg. Johann von Bohnenberger received the royal surveying commission in 1818. A mathematician and astronomer at Tübingen University, he placed the reference point for his measurements at the top of the castle’s north-east tower.

His measuring instrument stood elsewhere, beneath the little dome on the bastion. Bohnenberger had this observatory built in 1814 for a large repeating circle, one of the most advanced angle-measuring instruments of its day. The dome could rotate. The instrument thus occupied a room built specifically for its work on the castle bastion.

After Bohnenberger died in 1831, the small observatory fell into obscurity. Almost two centuries after its construction, Tübingen researcher Alfons Renz rediscovered the original instrument there in 2002. More than a historic building had survived: the almost complete repeating circle remained at its original location.

The state heritage authority restored the equipment, while the observatory itself was renovated. The Reichenbach repeating circle returned in 2018, for the two-hundredth anniversary of the start of Württemberg’s survey.

The work undertaken here extended well beyond the castle hill. Bohnenberger’s commission concerned the entire kingdom. The small dome on the bastion and the reference point on the tower belonged to that shared undertaking.

factCards.title: Schlosslabor: DNA from used bandages
factCards.short_description: In the Schlosslabor at Hohentübingen, Friedrich Miescher discovered the substance we now call DNA in 1869. His starting material was used wound dressings from Tübingen’s hospital. He extracted white blood cells from the pus and examined their nuclei, naming the unfamiliar substance nuclein. He did not yet know its role in heredity. His teacher Felix Hoppe-Seyler checked the findings himself before they were published in 1871. The discovery thus began in a converted castle kitchen, with unappealing material and careful verification rather than immediate certainty.
factCards.deep_dive_text:
At the Schlosslabor in Hohentübingen, Friedrich Miescher began studying white blood cells in autumn 1868. The university had converted the former castle kitchen into a chemical laboratory in 1818. Researchers here investigated chemical processes in living organisms. Felix Hoppe-Seyler, appointed professor in Tübingen in 1861, studied the red pigment in blood and named it haemoglobin.

Miescher needed many cells for his experiments. He collected used wound dressings from the hospital and washed white blood cells out of the pus. Early in 1869, he found a previously unknown substance in the cell nuclei. He called it nuclein, after the Latin word for nucleus. To examine it more closely, he used pepsin extracted from pigs’ stomachs. The enzyme broke down proteins, allowing the nuclear substance to be isolated.

Analysis revealed a high phosphorus content. Miescher did not know that the substance carried hereditary information. His teacher did not simply accept the result either: Hoppe-Seyler checked the experiments. Miescher’s work was not published until 1871.

An original preparation made by Miescher survives in the museum. It probably dates from around 1871, when he continued his research in Basel using Rhine salmon. Its label reads “Nuclein aus Lachssperma / F. Miescher”, meaning nuclein from salmon sperm. He had changed his starting material. The small vessel belongs to the continuation of work that began in Tübingen with used bandages.

factCards.title: Spital: charity and a paid place in old age
factCards.short_description: Tübingen’s Spital was a charitable institution for people with very different needs. The poor, the sick, travellers and abandoned children were meant to receive help here. The counts palatine founded it around 1260/70. By the late Middle Ages, its emphasis had shifted. Wealthy townspeople could buy a place as pensioners and secure care in old age. The long, plastered timber-framed building dates from the early sixteenth century, with further buildings around a courtyard behind it. The complex tells a story of public charity and provision made possible by private wealth.
factCards.deep_dive_text:
The Spital in Tübingen’s old town originally had a broad charitable purpose. It was meant to shelter the poor and feed the hungry and thirsty. Travellers needed accommodation, sick people needed care, poor women were to receive help in childbirth, and abandoned children were to be brought up. This description of its duties belongs to its thirteenth-century beginnings. The counts palatine of Tübingen founded the institution around 1260/70.

The long, two-storey building visible today is younger. It dates from the early sixteenth century and has a plastered timber frame. Together with buildings behind it, it forms a complex around an inner courtyard. Barns, stables and service buildings also belonged to the Spital. Its operation extended beyond the house seen from the street.

During the late Middle Ages, the institution changed character. Wealthy citizens bought places as pensioners, known as Pfründner, securing support and care in old age. An institution conceived around wide-ranging charitable duties became a home for people able to pay for that provision.

The Spital houses the Bürgerheim elderly care centre. Supporting older people has remained one of the purposes of this site. The courtyard complex still helps explain why this was a substantial civic institution rather than a single private home.

factCards.title: Kornhaus: grain trading becomes city history
factCards.short_description: The Kornhaus has housed Tübingen’s city museum since 1991, but it was built for very different purposes. Grain was stored and traded below, while townspeople gathered for social occasions upstairs. Schoolchildren later used the building, followed by the fire brigade and Red Cross. Today, the museum also explores Lotte Reiniger’s work. The animation pioneer made films using cut-paper silhouettes from the 1920s onwards. The former commercial building and her delicate film technique tell history at different scales: through the uses of a civic building and through an individual’s creative work.
factCards.deep_dive_text:
The Stadtmuseum occupies the Kornhaus, a building that served the town in several ways over many centuries. Its western part was built in 1453, with the eastern part following about fifty years later. An earlier building on the site had been destroyed by a town fire. The Kornhaus is one of Tübingen’s old utilitarian buildings in the Alemannic timber-framing tradition.

Grain was traded on the lower floor. By the seventeenth century, the upper rooms were used for dancing and social gatherings. Visiting actors also performed plays here. An extra storey had been added in 1604.

A primary school occupied the building in the nineteenth century, teaching children of winegrowers and craftspeople from the lower town. From 1892, the fire brigade and Red Cross used the Kornhaus. Between 1985 and 1991, it was converted into the city museum.

An exhibition about Lotte Reiniger explores the animation pioneer’s silhouette films, which she began making in the 1920s. Her figures involve a very different craft from the building’s timber frame, but both direct attention to constructed forms. Alongside artistic subjects, the museum addresses city history and contemporary questions. The Kornhaus’s own changing uses provide a useful starting point: grain market, meeting place, school and museum occupied the same rooms in succession.

factCards.title: Sternwarte: Carl Bosch’s telescope in Tübingen
factCards.short_description: The observatory on the Waldhäuser Höhe uses a telescope with an earlier life in Heidelberg. Built in 1925, the Zeiss refractor served Nobel laureate Carl Bosch for many years. It has been used to observe the night sky in Tübingen since 1956. Its objective is thirty centimetres across and its focal length is five metres. University astronomy reaches back much further: Johannes Stöffler became its first astronomy teacher in 1507. The telescope belongs to a long local tradition, but arrived as an instrument already used in another city.
factCards.deep_dive_text:
Tübingen’s observatory on the Waldhäuser Höhe combines public skywatching with the history of an older instrument. Its Zeiss refractor was constructed in 1925. Before coming to Tübingen, it served Carl Bosch in Heidelberg as an observing telescope for many years.

The instrument has been used for observations in Tübingen since 1956. Its objective measures thirty centimetres in diameter, and its focal length is five metres. Those measurements describe a particular surviving instrument rather than simply commemorating earlier astronomers.

The university’s astronomical history begins much earlier. In 1507, Johannes Stöffler was appointed its first astronomy teacher in the Arts Faculty. Centuries separate that early teaching from the Zeiss telescope.

The Astronomische Vereinigung organises talks and observing activities at the observatory. Whether looking through a telescope is possible also depends on the weather. The sky forms part of the programme, but cannot be made to follow an events calendar.

factCards.title: Ugge Bärtle: the workshop behind the city’s figures
factCards.short_description: The Ugge-Bärtle-Haus on Herrenberger Straße leads back to the sculptor whose work stands in several Tübingen public spaces. Eugen Bärtle, known as Ugge, worked stone with a point chisel and hammer. After training and years in Munich and Hamburg, he returned to Tübingen in 1949. He founded the Ellipse artists’ association and later helped initiate the Tübinger Künstlerbund. His studio and sculpture garden largely survive. Visitors who have seen his winegrower or the lion outside the technical town hall encounter the workplace behind those public figures here.
factCards.deep_dive_text:
The Ugge-Bärtle-Haus at Herrenberger Straße 12 was the home and workshop of Tübingen sculptor Eugen Bärtle, known as Ugge. He worked his sculptures out of stone using a point chisel and hammer. The surviving studio area and sculpture garden connect visitors with this practical side of his work.

Bärtle first trained as a stonemason in Tübingen, then studied at the art academy in Munich and spent further years in Hamburg. He returned to his home town in 1949. In the post-war period he founded the Ellipse artists’ association, active from 1951 to 1965. In 1971, he joined others in initiating the Tübinger Künstlerbund, helping artists organise collectively within the city.

Two public figures show the different tasks his sculptures performed. The shell-limestone winegrower of 1961 stands in Salzstadelgasse but was originally a fountain sculpture at Krumme Brücke. The city wanted a monument to its winegrowers. The lion of 1954 outside the technical town hall was carved from granite and designed as a guardian for the entrance.

factCards.title: Zoological collection: animals arranged by origin
factCards.short_description: Tübingen University’s zoological display collection occupies two levels. Upstairs, animals of Central Europe take centre stage; downstairs, specimens from other continents are arranged by geographical origin. Some preparations are more than a hundred years old. Certain specimens were gifts from Württemberg’s royal family, whose members brought animals back from their excursions. Birds and other vertebrates share the collection with insects, snails and mussels. The display also presents ways of ordering nature: by animal group, by origin and through holdings assembled over a long period.
factCards.deep_dive_text:
Tübingen University’s zoological display collection is arranged across two exhibition levels. The upper hall, “Tiere der Heimat”, focuses on Central Europe. Nearly all of the region’s more than three hundred native bird species are represented. Other vertebrates appear alongside insect groups large enough to be readily seen with the naked eye.

Other displays direct attention towards habitats and the traces animals leave. Forest pests appear with examples of their feeding damage, while another display concerns fish living in the Neckar or formerly found there. Feeding marks turn attention from an animal’s body to the effect of its activity. The Neckar display instead takes a particular river and its fauna as its subject.

On the ground floor, specimens are grouped by geographical origin. Selected animals represent Australia, Africa, Asia and the Americas. The oldest preparations are more than a hundred years old. Some were gifts from Württemberg’s royal family, whose members brought animals home from excursions. The collection therefore has a history of collecting as well as a zoological purpose.

Local and overseas snails and mussels add another group of objects. Moving through the two levels means moving between different arrangements: regional animals and habitats, then origins on different continents. Those choices show how the university makes assembled holdings available for observation and comparison.

factCards.title: Neptun und die Bürger am Marktplatz
factCards.short_description: Auf dem Tübinger Marktplatz steht Neptun über einem Brunnen, dessen Geschichte bis nach Bologna führt. Heinrich Schickhardt entwarf ihn nach dem dortigen Vorbild; 1617 führte Georg Müller die Arbeit aus. Der alte Sandstein verwitterte im Lauf der Jahrhunderte. Die heutige Fassung geht auf eine Neugestaltung von 1948 zurück, die fast vollständig durch Spenden aus der Bürgerschaft finanziert wurde. In den Wasserrohren sind sogar Köpfe von Beteiligten dargestellt. Zwischen den hohen Häusern des Platzes steht damit ein Kunstwerk, an dem sich die Tübinger selbst beteiligt haben, lange nach seiner ursprünglichen Entstehung.
factCards.deep_dive_text:
Der Marktplatz wird 1302 erstmals schriftlich erwähnt, Händler sind in Tübingen schon für 1191 belegt. Die hohen Häuser ringsum stammen überwiegend aus dem 15. und 16. Jahrhundert. Der Platz blieb ein Ort des Handels. Zum Wochenmarkt kommen die Treffen am Brunnen, besonders an warmen Sommerabenden.

Der Neptunbrunnen entstand nach einer Vorlage, die Heinrich Schickhardt auf einer Italienreise in Bologna skizziert hatte. Den Entwurf führte der Stuttgarter Bildhauer Georg Müller 1617 aus. Neptun trägt seinen Dreizack, die Frauenfiguren an seinem Fuß stehen für die vier Jahreszeiten. So kamen der römische Wassergott und die Jahreszeiten gemeinsam auf den Tübinger Marktplatz.

Vom ursprünglichen Sandstein sind Reste im Stadtmuseum erhalten. Nach dem Zweiten Weltkrieg arbeiteten Stadtverwaltung, Bürgerschaft und französische Militärregierung gemeinsam an der Neugestaltung. Die Fassung von 1948 war die erste städtische Bauaufgabe nach dem Krieg, die allein künstlerischen Zwecken diente. Finanziert wurde sie fast ausschließlich durch Bürgerspenden. Kopfprofile im Rankenwerk der Wasserrohre erinnern an Beteiligte.

Auch Literaturgeschichte gehört zum Platz. Wo heute ein Café und Restaurant Gäste empfängt, wohnte Hermann Kurz bis zu seinem Tod. Seine Tochter Isolde Kurz verbrachte hier einen Teil ihrer Jugend. Der Markt war damit zugleich Handelsplatz, Wohnort und später Schauplatz gemeinsamer Wiederherstellung.

factCards.title: Neckarfront: Universität am Fluss
factCards.short_description: An der Tübinger Neckarfront stehen die Gebäude der alten Universitätsstadt dicht beieinander. Von der Neckarbrücke aus folgen flussaufwärts Stiftskirche, Hölderlinturm, Burse, Evangelisches Stift und Schloss Hohentübingen. Hinter dieser vertrauten Ansicht liegen sehr verschiedene Lebensgeschichten. Hölderlin studierte im Stift, wurde später in der zur Klinik umgebauten Burse behandelt und lebte schließlich bei der Familie Zimmer im Turm. Häuser, die im Panorama fast zusammenrücken, gehörten für ihn zu ganz unterschiedlichen Lebensabschnitten. Die Neckarfront lässt sich deshalb auch als Weg durch ein Leben verstehen, nicht allein als hübsche Reihe alter Fassaden.
factCards.deep_dive_text:
Die Neckarfront zeigt, wie eng sich in Tübingen Stadtbefestigung, Wohnen und Universität räumlich überlagern. Schon im Mittelalter wurden Häuser auf der Stadtmauer am Neckar errichtet. Der Flussblick erfasst deshalb mehr als eine Reihe von Häuserfronten: Unter ihnen liegt ein Teil der früheren Befestigung.

Die Universitätsbauten hatten dabei keine unveränderlichen Aufgaben. Die Burse entstand von 1478 bis 1482 als Wohn- und Lehrhaus für Studenten. Von 1803 bis 1805 wurde sie zum ersten Tübinger Klinikum umgebaut. Heute sind dort Philosophie und Kunstgeschichte untergebracht. In der benachbarten Alten Aula kamen einst Bibliothek, Archiv und Hörsäle zusammen. Dort tagte auch der Senat, der akademische Grade verlieh und Strafen gegen Universitätsangehörige verhängen konnte.

Noch weiter oben nahm die Universität ein ehemaliges Herrschaftsgebäude in Besitz. König Wilhelm I. übertrug ihr 1816 das gesamte Schloss Hohentübingen. Eine Bibliothek zog zeitweise in den Rittersaal, eine Sternwarte in den Nordostturm und ein chemisches Labor in die Schlossküche.

Vom gegenüberliegenden Ufer und von der Platanenallee lassen sich diese Gebäude gemeinsam betrachten. Auf engem Raum wechselten dabei immer wieder die Aufgaben einzelner Häuser. Das Studentenwohnhaus wurde zur Klinik, die Küche zum Labor, das Schloss zum Universitätsstandort. Gerade diese konkreten Wechsel geben dem Panorama seine Geschichte.

factCards.title: Rathaus: eine Uhr für Sonne und Mond
factCards.short_description: Am Tübinger Rathaus zeigt eine Uhr mehr als die Tageszeit. Johannes Stöffler schuf 1511 die astronomische Uhr mit Anzeigen für Sonne, Mond und den sogenannten Drachenzeiger. Das ursprüngliche Ziffernblatt mit den Tierkreiszeichen liegt heute im Stadtmuseum. Die Uhr selbst wurde 1849 in den Ziergiebel versetzt. Auch die bemalte Fassade ist jünger als das Rathaus von 1435: Sie erhielt ihre heutige Gestaltung zum Universitätsjubiläum 1877. Wer das Gebäude betrachtet, sieht deshalb nicht einfach ein mittelalterliches Rathaus, sondern mehrere Umbauten, mit denen verschiedene Generationen das öffentliche Gesicht ihrer Stadt verändert haben.
factCards.deep_dive_text:
Das Rathaus am Marktplatz war zugleich Verwaltungsbau, Gericht und Handelsort. Im mittelalterlichen Erdgeschoss lagen das städtische Salzlager und ein Gefängnis. In einer offenen Arkadenhalle verkauften Bäcker und Metzger ihre Waren. Der Große Saal im ersten Stock diente den Gerbern als Verkaufsraum. Gericht und Rat tagten darüber. Diese Verteilung brachte Alltagsgeschäfte und städtische Macht in einem Haus zusammen.

Die astronomische Uhr von Johannes Stöffler kam 1511 hinzu. Ihr ursprüngliches Ziffernblatt mit Tierkreiszeichen wird im Stadtmuseum aufbewahrt. Seit ihrer Versetzung 1849 sitzt die Uhr im Ziergiebel. Neben der Stundenanzeige verzeichnet das astronomische Ziffernblatt mit seinen drei Zeigern Datum, Mondphasen und bestimmte Himmelsereignisse.

Die Fassade wurde 1877 zum 400. Jubiläum der Universität in einem Stil der Neorenaissance neu gestaltet. Zu den Figuren am Gebäude gehört eine Bacchantin an der Südostecke. Die Anhängerin des Weingottes Bacchus verweist auf die frühere Bedeutung des Weinbaus.

Auch innen wurde Geschichte verändert und später wieder sichtbar gemacht. Der historische Hofgerichtssaal hatte zwischenzeitlich Büros weichen müssen. Bei den Sanierungen von 2012 bis 2015 stellte man den Raum wieder her. Seine heutige Wandbemalung rekonstruiert eine Fassung aus den 1920er-Jahren, die beim Abbruch der Bürowände zum Vorschein kam. Nicht alles Historische im Rathaus stammt also aus seiner Erbauungszeit.

factCards.title: Schloss Hohentübingen: Forschung in der Schlossküche
factCards.short_description: Im Schloss Hohentübingen wurde eine Küche zum Forschungslabor. Die Universität richtete dort 1818 ein chemisches Labor ein; 1869 entdeckte Friedrich Miescher hier eine Substanz aus Zellkernen, die er „Nuklein“ nannte. Ihre Funktion als Träger der Erbinformation war ihm noch nicht bekannt. Die Forschung zog in ein Gebäude mit ganz anderer Vergangenheit: Hohentübingen wurde 1078 als Burg erwähnt und später zur Renaissanceanlage umgebaut. König Wilhelm I. überließ 1816 das gesamte Schloss der Universität. Damit fanden zwischen den Mauern einer ehemaligen Residenz auch Bibliothek, Sternwarte und Labor Platz.
factCards.deep_dive_text:
Schloss Hohentübingen verbindet eine Herrschaftsgeschichte mit der Geschichte experimenteller Forschung. Die Herren von Tübingen verkauften Burg und Stadt 1342 an die Grafen von Württemberg. Die heutige Vierflügelanlage mit Rundtürmen ist von der Renaissance geprägt. Nachdem die Universität bereits einzelne Räume übernommen hatte, erhielt sie 1816 das ganze Schloss. Seine Räume bekamen neue Aufgaben: Der Rittersaal beherbergte zeitweise eine Bibliothek, der Nordostturm eine Sternwarte.

In der ehemaligen Küche entstand 1818 ein chemisches Labor. Dort untersuchte Friedrich Miescher ab Herbst 1868 weiße Blutkörperchen. Das Material gewann er aus gebrauchten Wundverbänden des Tübinger Krankenhauses: Er wusch die Zellen aus dem Eiter heraus. Anfang 1869 isolierte er in den Zellkernen eine unbekannte Substanz. Mit Pepsin aus Schweinemägen zerlegte er die Proteine, um das „Nuklein“ genauer untersuchen zu können.

Miescher stellte einen hohen Phosphorgehalt fest. Was die Substanz für die Vererbung bedeutete, wusste er noch nicht. Sein Lehrer Felix Hoppe-Seyler prüfte die Ergebnisse zunächst selbst; veröffentlicht wurde die Arbeit erst 1871.

Ein Originalpräparat von Mieschers Hand ist heute im Schlosslabor ausgestellt. Es entstand vermutlich um 1871 in Basel, wo er mit Lachsen weiterforschte. Auf dem Glas steht „Nuclein aus Lachssperma / F. Miescher“. Seine Forschung ging also nach der Tübinger Entdeckung weiter.

factCards.title: Stocherkähne: vom eigenen Boot zur öffentlichen Fahrt
factCards.short_description: Die Tübinger Stocherkähne gehören zum Neckar vor der Altstadt. Dass heute auch Menschen ohne eigenes Boot mitfahren können, war nicht immer selbstverständlich. Lange blieb das Kahnfahren den Besitzern vorbehalten, darunter vor allem Studentenverbindungen. In den 1980er-Jahren bot der Bürger- und Verkehrsverein erstmals einen Stocherkahn auf Bestellung für alle an. Damit wurde aus einem Vergnügen für einen begrenzten Kreis ein öffentlich zugängliches Angebot. Die Fahrt führt an der Neckarfront entlang, vorbei an Hölderlinturm, Burse und Evangelischem Stift. Die große Anlegestelle liegt am Ufer beim Hölderlinturm.
factCards.deep_dive_text:
Bei den Stocherkähnen am Neckar ist die Frage des Zugangs ein Teil der Geschichte. Lange Zeit durfte nur fahren, wer einen eigenen Kahn besaß. Besonders die Studentenverbindungen verfügten über solche Boote. Ein öffentlich buchbares Angebot war das noch nicht.

Der Bürger- und Verkehrsverein änderte dies in den 1980er-Jahren mit Fahrten auf Bestellung. Die Entwicklung erklärt, weshalb das Kahnfahren sowohl mit studentischen Traditionen als auch mit dem heutigen Tourismus verbunden ist. Auch die Tübinger selbst nutzen die Fahrten als Freizeitvergnügen auf ihrem Fluss.

factCards.title: Französisches Viertel: Alltag nach den Kasernen
factCards.short_description: Das Französische Viertel entstand nach dem Abzug französischer Truppen 1991/92 auf ehemaligem Militärgelände. Tübingen nutzte die Fläche für ein Quartier, in dem Wohnen, Arbeit, Versorgung und Kultur nah beieinanderliegen. Alte Militärgebäude wurden in drei- bis fünfgeschossige Wohnblöcke integriert. Das Konzept gab Fußwegen, Radverkehr und öffentlichem Verkehr Vorrang vor dem Auto und erhielt 2001 den Deutschen Städtebaupreis. An der Panzerhalle zeigt sogar eine Skulptur den Grundriss des Viertels: Sechsundzwanzig Jugendliche schufen sie 2004 unter Anleitung von Jürgen Klugmann. Hier wurde Stadtplanung auch zum Gegenstand gemeinsamer künstlerischer Arbeit.

Das Französische Viertel ist aus einer militärischen Brache entstanden. Als die französischen Truppen 1991/92 abzogen, konnte Tübingen im Süden der Stadt größere Flächen neu nutzen. Auf dem insgesamt etwa sechzig Hektar großen Gelände entwickelten sich das Französische Viertel und das Loretto-Areal. Diese Flächenangabe bezieht sich auf beide Quartiere zusammen, nicht allein auf das Französische Viertel.

Die Planung setzte auf kurze Wege. Wohnen, Arbeiten, Versorgung und Kultur sollten eng verbunden sein. In drei- bis fünfgeschossige Wohnblöcke wurden ehemalige Militärgebäude einbezogen. Statt einer neuen Siedlung auf der grünen Wiese entstand ein gemischtes Viertel auf bereits genutztem Gelände. Soziale Vielfalt und der Vorrang für nicht motorisierten und öffentlichen Verkehr gehörten zum Konzept. Der Deutsche Städtebaupreis 2001 würdigte diese Entwicklung.

Ein Kunstwerk an der Panzerhalle macht den Plan des Viertels selbst zum Motiv. Die Metallplastik aus Cortenstahl entstand 2004. Sechsundzwanzig Jugendliche arbeiteten unter Anleitung von Jürgen Klugmann daran; die Form zeigt den Grundriss des Französischen Viertels. Das Projekt hieß „Ein Kunstwerk für die Südstadt“.

Wer zwischen den Gebäuden unterwegs ist, kann damit zwei Maßstäbe vergleichen: das Viertel als bewohnten Raum und seinen Grundriss als Skulptur. Die frühere militärische Nutzung ist in erhaltenen Gebäuden noch Teil der neuen Stadtstruktur, während die Nutzungen auf den zivilen Alltag ausgerichtet wurden.

factCards.title: Kunsthalle: Ausstellungen, die wechseln
factCards.short_description: Die Kunsthalle Tübingen ist ein Haus für wechselnde Ausstellungen zur Kunst des zwanzigsten und einundzwanzigsten Jahrhunderts. Mal steht eine einzelne künstlerische Position im Mittelpunkt, mal eine Frage, die Werke aus verschiedenen Zeiten zusammenbringt. Auch private Sammlungen moderner und zeitgenössischer Kunst gehören zum Programm. Das bedeutet für einen Besuch: Entscheidend ist die jeweilige Ausstellung, nicht die Erwartung, immer dieselben Bilder anzutreffen. Die Kunsthalle setzt außerdem auf Vermittlung zum Mitmachen und auf Angebote für unterschiedliche Generationen. Welche Werke gerade zu sehen sind, muss das aktuelle Programm beantworten.
factCards.deep_dive_text:
Die Kunsthalle Tübingen arbeitet mit Wechselausstellungen. Manche widmen sich einer einzelnen künstlerischen Position des zwanzigsten oder einundzwanzigsten Jahrhunderts. Andere nehmen eine Frage zum Ausgangspunkt und bringen dafür Werke aus unterschiedlichen Epochen zusammen.

Dabei geht es sowohl um künstlerische als auch um gesellschaftliche Themen. Eine solche Zusammenstellung erlaubt Vergleiche, die in einer streng nach Entstehungszeit geordneten Schau anders ausfallen würden. Präsentationen privater Sammlungen moderner und zeitgenössischer Kunst ergänzen das Programm.

Zur Arbeit des Hauses gehört auch interaktive und generationenübergreifende Vermittlung. Menschen mit unterschiedlicher Vorerfahrung sollen sich mit den Werken beschäftigen können. Die Kunsthalle verbindet den Wechsel ihrer Ausstellungen also mit verschiedenen Wegen, die ausgestellte Kunst gemeinsam zu betrachten und darüber zu sprechen.

factCards.title: MUT Alte Kulturen: das Pferd aus Mammutelfenbein
factCards.short_description: Im Museum Alte Kulturen auf Schloss Hohentübingen gehören Figuren aus Mammutelfenbein zu den bekanntesten Objekten. Vor rund vierzigtausend Jahren schnitzten Menschen auf der Schwäbischen Alb Tiere wie Pferde, Mammuts und Höhlenlöwen. Das Vogelherdpferdchen ist eines dieser erhaltenen Werke. Die betreffenden Höhlen wurden 2017 UNESCO-Welterbe. Im Schloss begegnen diese kleinen Originale anderen Zeugnissen menschlicher Gestaltung, darunter einer altägyptischen Opferkammer und antiken Skulpturen. Die Ausstellung verbindet mehrere archäologische und kulturwissenschaftliche Universitätssammlungen. Ihr Ausgangspunkt sind konkrete Gegenstände: geschnitzt, geformt und über sehr unterschiedliche Zeiträume erhalten.
factCards.deep_dive_text:
Das Museum Alte Kulturen im Schloss Hohentübingen zeigt archäologische und kulturwissenschaftliche Sammlungen der Universität. Besonders bekannt sind die Vogelherd-Figuren. Menschen schnitzten vor rund vierzigtausend Jahren Tiere aus Mammutelfenbein, darunter Wildpferde, Mammuts und Höhlenlöwen. Das Vogelherdpferdchen gehört zu diesen erhaltenen frühen Kunstwerken.

Die Objekte kommen aus den Eiszeithöhlen der Schwäbischen Alb. 2017 nahm die UNESCO sechs Höhlen mit dieser Eiszeitkunst in die Welterbeliste auf. Im Schloss lassen sich Originalfunde betrachten, also die bearbeiteten Gegenstände selbst. Auch das Fragment einer Flöte aus Gänsegeierknochen gehört zur Schau. Damit tritt neben die bildliche Darstellung von Tieren ein Zeugnis früher Musik.

Die Ausstellung reicht aber über die Eiszeit hinaus. Zu den weiteren Objekten gehören der Tübinger Waffenläufer, eine altägyptische Opferkammer und die antiken Skulpturen der Glyptothek im Rittersaal. Verschiedene Materialien und Formen stehen so innerhalb eines Hauses nebeneinander, ohne aus derselben Epoche zu stammen.

Die Präsentation verteilt sich auf zweitausend Quadratmeter und umfasst rund viertausendsechshundert Objekte aus sieben Sammlungen. Diese Zahlen beschreiben den Umfang des Museums, nicht einen sinnvollen Pflichtweg. Beim Besuch kann ein einzelnes Tier aus Elfenbein der genauere Ausgangspunkt sein: Seine Form lässt sich betrachten, bevor der Blick zu den größeren Objekten und den späteren Kulturen weitergeht.

factCards.title: Botanischer Garten: Forschung unter freiem Himmel
factCards.short_description: Der Botanische Garten auf der Morgenstelle wurde 1968 eröffnet und gehört zur Forschung und Lehre der Universität Tübingen. Zugleich ist er ein Ort zum Spazieren und Schauen. Etwa zehntausend Pflanzenarten wachsen hier auf zehn Hektar. Draußen führen Wege durch unterschiedliche Gartenbereiche; in den Gewächshäusern stehen tropische Pflanzen. Jenseits des Nordrings liegt außerdem das Arboretum mit seltenen Bäumen. Wer hier geht, bewegt sich durch eine wissenschaftliche Sammlung lebender Pflanzen. Der Garten hat eine andere Aufgabe als ein reiner Stadtpark, auch wenn man in beiden eine Pause machen kann.
factCards.deep_dive_text:
Der Botanische Garten der Universität Tübingen auf der Morgenstelle eröffnete 1968. Er ist eine Einrichtung für Forschung und Lehre und zugleich ein Schau- und Erholungsgarten. Wer durch die Anlage geht, bewegt sich durch eine lebende Sammlung von rund zehntausend Pflanzenarten auf zehn Hektar.

Die Gartenbereiche reichen von Pflanzenwelten der Alpen bis zu tropischen Beständen in den Gewächshäusern. Ein Gang durch das Freiland und der Blick in ein Gewächshaus zeigen deshalb unterschiedliche Teile derselben Sammlung. Jenseits des Nordrings liegt außerdem das Arboretum mit seinen seltenen Bäumen.

Auch das Gelände unterhalb des Gartens gehört zu einem möglichen Spaziergang: Im Käsenbachtal liegt das Elysium mit dem geografischen Mittelpunkt Baden-Württembergs. Von dort geht es hinauf zum Garten auf der Morgenstelle. Aus dem Tal erreicht man damit eine Anlage, in der Erholung und universitäre Pflanzenkunde denselben Raum nutzen.

factCards.title: Schloss-Sternwarte: Württemberg vermessen
factCards.short_description: Die Schloss-Sternwarte gehört zu einer Geschichte präziser Winkelmessung: Johann von Bohnenberger erhielt 1818 den Auftrag, Württemberg zu vermessen. Den Nullpunkt legte er auf die Spitze des Nordostturms von Schloss Hohentübingen. Für sein Messinstrument hatte er bereits 1814 auf der Bastion ein kleines Observatorium mit drehbarer Kuppel bauen lassen. Dort entdeckte der Wissenschaftler Alfons Renz 2002 das originale Gerät wieder. Nach der Restaurierung kehrte der Reichenbach’sche Wiederholungskreis 2018 an seinen Aufstellungsort zurück. Hinter der kleinen Kuppel steckt damit auch die Geschichte der Karten, mit denen Land vermessen und beschrieben wurde.
factCards.deep_dive_text:
Die Schloss-Sternwarte auf Hohentübingen gehört zur Vermessungsgeschichte Württembergs. Johann von Bohnenberger erhielt 1818 den königlichen Auftrag zur Landesvermessung. Er war Mathematiker und Astronom an der Universität Tübingen und legte den Nullpunkt seiner Messungen auf die Spitze des Nordostturms.

Unter der kleinen Kuppel auf der Bastion stand dagegen sein Messinstrument: der große Wiederholungskreis. Bohnenberger hatte dieses Observatorium bereits 1814 errichten lassen. Der Kreis gehörte zu den modernsten Winkelmessgeräten seiner Zeit. Die Kuppel ließ sich drehen. So erhielt das Instrument einen eigens für seine Arbeit gebauten Raum auf der Schlossbastion.

Nach Bohnenbergers Tod 1831 geriet die kleine Sternwarte in Vergessenheit. Fast zwei Jahrhunderte nach ihrem Bau fand der Tübinger Wissenschaftler Alfons Renz dort 2002 das Originalgerät wieder. Das war mehr als die Wiederentdeckung eines historischen Gebäudes: Auch der nahezu vollständige Wiederholungskreis war an seinem ursprünglichen Aufstellungsort erhalten geblieben.

Das Landesamt für Denkmalpflege restaurierte das Gerät. Währenddessen wurde auch das Observatorium saniert. 2018 kehrte der Reichenbach’sche Wiederholungskreis zurück, zum zweihundertjährigen Jubiläum des Beginns der württembergischen Landesvermessung.

Vom Schloss aus ging es bei dieser Arbeit weit über den Schlossberg hinaus: Bohnenbergers Auftrag galt dem ganzen Königreich. Die kleine Kuppel auf der Bastion und der Bezugspunkt oben am Turm gehören zu diesem gemeinsamen Vorhaben.

factCards.title: Schlosslabor: DNA aus gebrauchten Verbänden
factCards.short_description: Im Schlosslabor von Hohentübingen entdeckte Friedrich Miescher 1869 die Substanz, die wir heute DNA nennen. Sein Ausgangsmaterial waren benutzte Wundverbände aus dem Tübinger Krankenhaus. Aus dem Eiter gewann er weiße Blutkörperchen und untersuchte ihre Zellkerne. Den unbekannten Stoff nannte er Nuklein. Welche Bedeutung er für die Vererbung hatte, konnte Miescher damals noch nicht wissen. Sein Lehrer Felix Hoppe-Seyler prüfte die Ergebnisse zunächst selbst; veröffentlicht wurden sie erst 1871. factCards.title: Kornhaus: erst Getreide, dann Stadtgeschichte
factCards.short_description: Das Kornhaus beherbergt seit 1991 das Tübinger Stadtmuseum, wurde aber für ganz andere Aufgaben gebaut. Unten lagerte und handelte man Getreide, oben trafen sich Bürger zu geselligen Veranstaltungen. Später kamen Schulkinder, dann Feuerwehr und Rotes Kreuz ins Haus. Heute gehört Lotte Reiniger zu den Themen des Museums. Die Trickfilmpionierin schuf seit den zwanziger Jahren Filme mit Scherenschnitten. Zwischen dem alten Wirtschaftsgebäude und ihrer filigranen Filmtechnik liegt ein deutlicher Maßstabswechsel: Das Haus erzählt Tübinger Geschichte sowohl durch seine eigene Nutzung als auch durch die Menschen, deren Arbeit es zeigt.
factCards.deep_dive_text:
Das Stadtmuseum im Kornhaus nutzt ein Gebäude, das über Jahrhunderte Aufgaben für die Stadt übernommen hat. Der westliche Teil entstand 1453, der östliche etwa fünfzig Jahre später. Schon zuvor hatte an dieser Stelle ein Bau gestanden, der bei einem Stadtbrand zerstört wurde. Das Kornhaus gehört zu Tübingens alten Nutzbauten in alemannischer Fachwerkbauweise.

Im unteren Geschoss fand Getreidehandel statt. Die Räume darüber dienten bereits im siebzehnten Jahrhundert als Bürgerhaus für Tanz und gesellschaftliche Veranstaltungen. Reisende Komödianten spielten hier auch Theater. 1604 war das Haus um ein Geschoss aufgestockt worden.

Im neunzehnten Jahrhundert zog eine Volksschule ein. Sie wurde von Kindern der Weingärtner und Handwerker aus der Unterstadt besucht. Ab 1892 nutzten Feuerwehr und Rotes Kreuz das Kornhaus. Zwischen 1985 und 1991 wurde es zum Stadtmuseum umgebaut.

Zur Museumsarbeit gehört eine Ausstellung über Lotte Reiniger, die seit den zwanziger Jahren mit Scherenschnittfilmen arbeitete. Ihre Figuren gehören zu einer anderen Art von Handwerk als das Fachwerk des Hauses, doch beides lenkt den Blick auf gemachte Formen. Neben solchen künstlerischen Themen behandelt das Museum auch Stadtgeschichte und aktuelle Fragen. Für einen Gang durch das Kornhaus ist seine eigene Nutzungsgeschichte ein guter Anfang: Markt, gesellschaftlicher Treffpunkt, Schule und schließlich Museum haben nacheinander dieselben Räume gebraucht.

factCards.title: Neptune and the people of the Marktplatz
factCards.short_description: Neptune stands above a fountain on Tübingen’s Marktplatz with a history reaching back to Bologna. Heinrich Schickhardt designed it after the fountain there; Georg Müller executed the work in 1617. Over the centuries, the original sandstone deteriorated. The present version dates to a reconstruction in 1948, funded almost entirely by donations from local residents. Profiles of people involved even appear in the decorative water pipes. Among the square’s tall houses stands a work of art that the people of Tübingen helped remake, long after its original creation.
factCards.deep_dive_text:
The Marktplatz first appears in written records in 1302, while traders in Tübingen are documented as early as 1191. Most of the tall houses around the square date from the 15th and 16th centuries. Trade continued here. The weekly market shares the square with gatherings around the fountain, especially on warm summer evenings.

Heinrich Schickhardt based the Neptunbrunnen on a fountain he had sketched in Bologna during a journey through Italy. The Stuttgart sculptor Georg Müller executed his design in 1617. Neptune carries his trident, while the female figures at his feet represent the four seasons. The Roman water god and the seasons thus found a shared place on Tübingen’s market square.

Fragments of the original sandstone survive in the Stadtmuseum. After the Second World War, the municipal administration, residents and the French military government worked together on the reconstruction. The 1948 version was the first municipal building project after the war devoted solely to artistic purposes. Residents’ donations paid almost all the cost. Profiles in the decorative water pipes commemorate participants.

Literary history also belongs to the square. Hermann Kurz lived until his death in the house now occupied by a café and restaurant. His daughter Isolde Kurz spent part of her youth there. This was a place of trade, a home and, later, a site of collective restoration.

factCards.title: Neckarfront: a university beside the river
factCards.short_description: Tübingen’s Neckarfront brings the buildings of the old university town into a single view. Looking upstream from the Neckarbrücke, the sequence includes the Stiftskirche, Hölderlinturm, Burse, Evangelisches Stift and Schloss Hohentübingen. These neighbouring buildings held very different places in Friedrich Hölderlin’s life. He studied at the Stift, later received treatment in the Burse after it became a clinic, and finally lived with the Zimmer family in the tower. Buildings that seem close together in the panorama belonged to separate chapters of his life. The riverfront offers a way into those histories as well as a view of old façades.
factCards.deep_dive_text:
The Neckarfront brings Tübingen’s defences, homes and university into close proximity. Houses were already being built on the riverside town wall in the Middle Ages. Beneath the familiar façades is part of an earlier defensive structure.

The university buildings did not always have the same purpose. The Burse was built between 1478 and 1482 to accommodate and teach students. Between 1803 and 1805 it became Tübingen’s first university clinic. It now houses philosophy and art history. In the nearby Alte Aula, the university once kept its library and archive alongside lecture rooms. Its senate also met there to award degrees and impose penalties on members of the university.

Higher up the hill, academic life moved into a former seat of political power. In 1816, King Wilhelm I. transferred the whole of Schloss Hohentübingen to the university. For a time the library occupied the knights’ hall; an observatory was installed in the northeast tower and a chemical laboratory in the castle kitchen.

The opposite bank and the Platanenallee offer views that bring these buildings together. Within this compact space, individual buildings repeatedly acquired new uses. A student residence became a clinic, a kitchen became a laboratory, and a castle became university premises. Those specific changes give the panorama its history.

factCards.title: The Rathaus clock: more than the time
factCards.short_description: The clock on Tübingen’s Rathaus displays more than the time of day. Johannes Stöffler created the astronomical clock in 1511, with indicators for the sun, moon and the so-called dragon hand. Its original zodiac dial is now in the Stadtmuseum. The clock itself was moved into the decorative gable in 1849. The painted façade is also younger than the town hall, built in 1435: it received its present design for the university anniversary in 1877. The building combines several generations of changes to the town’s public face.
factCards.deep_dive_text:
The Rathaus on the Marktplatz combined administration, justice and trade. Its medieval ground floor contained the municipal salt store and a prison. Bakers and butchers sold their goods in an open arcade, while tanners used the large first-floor hall as a salesroom. The town court and council met above them. Everyday commerce and civic authority shared one building.

Johannes Stöffler’s astronomical clock was added in 1511. Its original dial, decorated with zodiac signs, is preserved in the Stadtmuseum. Following its relocation in 1849, the clock sits in the decorative gable. Beside the ordinary time display, the astronomical dial uses three hands to indicate the date, phases of the moon and certain celestial events.

The façade was redesigned in a Neo-Renaissance style in 1877 for the university’s 400th anniversary. One of the building’s figures is a Bacchantin on the southeast corner. This follower of Bacchus, the god of wine, refers to the former importance of winegrowing.

The interior has also been changed and partly recovered. Offices once replaced the historic ducal court hall. During renovation between 2012 and 2015, the room was restored. Its present wall decoration reconstructs a scheme from the 1920s, discovered when the office partitions came down. The historic-looking parts of the Rathaus do not all come from its original construction.

factCards.title: Schloss Hohentübingen: science in the castle kitchen
factCards.short_description: At Schloss Hohentübingen, a kitchen became a research laboratory. The university installed a chemical laboratory there in 1818. In 1869, Friedrich Miescher discovered a substance from cell nuclei that he called “Nuklein”. He did not yet know its role in carrying hereditary information. His research took place in a building with a very different past: Hohentübingen was recorded as a castle in 1078 and later rebuilt as a Renaissance complex. King Wilhelm I. transferred the whole castle to the university in 1816. A library, observatory and laboratory found space within the former residence.
factCards.deep_dive_text:
Schloss Hohentübingen connects the history of political rule with experimental science. The lords of Tübingen sold the castle and town to the counts of Württemberg in 1342. The present four-wing complex, with its round towers, is shaped by Renaissance rebuilding. After occupying individual rooms, the university received the entire castle in 1816. Rooms acquired new purposes: the knights’ hall housed a library for a time, and the northeast tower became an observatory.

A chemical laboratory opened in the former kitchen in 1818. Here Friedrich Miescher began studying white blood cells in autumn 1868. He obtained them from used wound dressings collected at the Tübingen hospital, washing the cells out of the pus. Early in 1869 he isolated an unknown substance from their nuclei. He used pepsin from pigs’ stomachs to break down proteins so that he could examine this “Nuklein” more closely.

Miescher identified a high phosphorus content. He did not yet understand what the substance meant for heredity. His teacher Felix Hoppe-Seyler checked the results himself, and publication followed only in 1871.

An original preparation made by Miescher is exhibited in the Schlosslabor today. It probably dates from around 1871 in Basel, where he continued his research using salmon. The glass is labelled “Nuclein aus Lachssperma / F. Miescher”. His work continued after the Tübingen discovery.

factCards.title: Stocherkähne: opening the boats to everyone
factCards.short_description: Tübingen’s Stocherkähne are part of life on the Neckar beside the old town. Being able to take a trip without owning a boat was not always a given. For a long time, boating was restricted to owners, especially student fraternities. In the 1980s, the Bürger- und Verkehrsverein began offering a Stocherkahn on request to anyone. An activity available to a limited circle became publicly bookable. Trips follow the Neckarfront past the Hölderlinturm, Burse and Evangelisches Stift. The main landing stage is on the riverbank beside the Hölderlinturm.
factCards.deep_dive_text:
Access is part of the history of the Stocherkähne on the Neckar. For a long time, only people who owned a boat were permitted to take one out. Student fraternities in particular had boats of their own. This was not yet a publicly bookable service.

The Bürger- und Verkehrsverein changed that in the 1980s by offering trips on request. This helps explain why boating here is associated both with student traditions and with tourism. Residents also enjoy the trips as a way to spend time on their river.

The landing stage beside the Hölderlinturm places the boats within the old town’s riverside setting. A trip from this bank can be combined with a walk through the Zwingel. From the water, the focus is on the buildings of the Neckarfront: the Stiftskirche, Hölderlinturm, Burse and Evangelisches Stift, with Schloss Hohentübingen above them.

factCards.title: Französisches Viertel: life after the barracks
factCards.short_description: The Französisches Viertel grew on former military land after French troops left in 1991/92. Tübingen used the site for a neighbourhood bringing homes, work, services and culture close together. Former military buildings were incorporated into residential blocks of three to five storeys. The concept prioritised walking, cycling and public transport and received the German Urban Development Award in 2001. Beside the Panzerhalle, a sculpture even depicts the neighbourhood’s ground plan. Twenty-six young people made it in 2004 under Jürgen Klugmann’s guidance, turning urban planning into a shared artistic project.
factCards.deep_dive_text:
The Französisches Viertel developed from a former military site. When French troops withdrew in 1991/92, Tübingen gained the opportunity to reuse substantial areas in the south of the city. The Französisches Viertel and Loretto-Areal developed on a combined site of about sixty hectares. That figure refers to both neighbourhoods together, not just the Französisches Viertel.

The plan aimed to keep everyday journeys short. Housing, work, services and culture were closely combined. Former military buildings became part of residential blocks with three to five storeys. Rather than building another settlement on undeveloped land, the city created a mixed neighbourhood on an already occupied site. Social diversity and priority for non-motorised and public transport formed part of the concept. The development received the German Urban Development Award in 2001.

An artwork beside the Panzerhalle makes the neighbourhood plan its subject. The Corten steel sculpture dates from 2004. Twenty-six young people worked on it under Jürgen Klugmann’s guidance, giving it the form of the neighbourhood’s ground plan. Their project was called “An artwork for the Südstadt”.

factCards.title: Kunsthalle: a museum of changing exhibitions
factCards.short_description: The Kunsthalle Tübingen presents changing exhibitions of twentieth- and twenty-first-century art. One exhibition may focus on a single artist; another may bring works from different periods together around a shared question. Private collections of modern and contemporary art also feature in its programme. For a visit, the particular exhibition matters more than expecting to find the same pictures every time. The Kunsthalle also uses participatory interpretation and activities across generations. Its current programme, rather than a permanent list of exhibits, determines what you can see.
factCards.deep_dive_text:
The Kunsthalle Tübingen works through changing exhibitions. Some focus on an individual artist of the twentieth or twenty-first century. Others begin with a question and bring together works from different periods to explore it.

The subjects include both artistic and social issues. Such arrangements invite comparisons that would look different in a display organised strictly by date. Presentations drawn from private collections of modern and contemporary art add another strand to the programme.

The institution also uses interactive interpretation and activities across generations. People with different levels of experience are encouraged to engage with the works. Changing exhibitions therefore go alongside different ways of looking at the art together and discussing it.

factCards.title: MUT Alte Kulturen: a horse carved in mammoth ivory
factCards.short_description: At the Museum Alte Kulturen in Schloss Hohentübingen, mammoth-ivory figures are among the best-known objects. Around forty thousand years ago, people on the Swabian Alb carved animals including horses, mammoths and cave lions. The Vogelherd horse is one surviving example. The associated caves became UNESCO World Heritage in 2017. Inside the castle, these small originals join other records of human craftsmanship, including an ancient Egyptian offering chamber and ancient sculpture. The exhibition brings together several university collections. Its starting points are tangible objects, carved or shaped and preserved across very different lengths of time.
factCards.deep_dive_text:
The Museum Alte Kulturen in Schloss Hohentübingen displays the university’s archaeological and cultural collections. The Vogelherd figures are particularly well known. Around forty thousand years ago, people carved animals from mammoth ivory, including wild horses, mammoths and cave lions. The Vogelherd horse is one of these surviving early artworks.

The objects come from Ice Age caves on the Swabian Alb. In 2017, UNESCO added six caves associated with this art to the World Heritage List. The castle displays original finds, meaning the worked objects themselves. A flute fragment made from griffon vulture bone also belongs to the display. Alongside representations of animals, there is therefore evidence of early music.

The exhibition extends beyond the Ice Age. Other objects include the Tübingen armed runner, an ancient Egyptian offering chamber and the ancient sculptures of the Glyptothek in the Knights’ Hall. Different materials and forms share one building without belonging to the same historical period.

The exhibition occupies two thousand square metres, with around four thousand six hundred objects from seven collections. These figures describe the museum’s scale, not a compulsory itinerary. One ivory animal can be a more manageable starting point: look at its shape before moving on to larger objects and later cultures.

factCards.title: Botanical garden: a living university collection
factCards.short_description: The botanical garden on the Morgenstelle opened in 1968 as part of Tübingen University’s research and teaching. It is also a place for walking and looking. Around ten thousand plant species grow here across ten hectares. Paths run through different outdoor sections, while greenhouses contain tropical plants. An arboretum with rare trees lies beyond the Nordring. Walking here means moving through a scientific collection of living plants. The garden has a different purpose from an ordinary city park, even though both can offer a place to pause.
factCards.deep_dive_text:
Tübingen University’s botanical garden on the Morgenstelle opened in 1968. It supports research and teaching while also providing a place for public display and recreation. A walk here passes through a living collection of around ten thousand plant species on ten hectares.

The garden’s sections range from Alpine plant life to tropical collections in the greenhouses. A walk outdoors and a look inside a greenhouse therefore reveal different parts of the same collection. Beyond the Nordring lies the arboretum with its rare trees.

The land below the garden also belongs to a possible longer walk. In the Käsenbach valley, the Elysium contains the geographical centre of Baden-Württemberg. From there, the route climbs towards the garden on the Morgenstelle. Leaving the valley brings you to a place where recreation and university botany share the same ground.

factCards.title: Schloss-Sternwarte: measuring Württemberg
factCards.short_description: The Schloss-Sternwarte belongs to a history of precise angle measurement. Johann von Bohnenberger was commissioned to survey Württemberg in 1818 and placed his reference point at the top of Schloss Hohentübingen’s north-east tower. For his measuring instrument, he had already built a small observatory with a rotating dome on the bastion in 1814. Researcher Alfons Renz rediscovered the original instrument there in 2002. After restoration, the Reichenbach repeating circle returned in 2018. The little dome thus also belongs to the history of maps used to measure and describe land.
factCards.deep_dive_text:
The Schloss-Sternwarte at Hohentübingen belongs to the history of surveying Württemberg. Johann von Bohnenberger received the royal surveying commission in 1818. A mathematician and astronomer at Tübingen University, he placed the reference point for his measurements at the top of the castle’s north-east tower.

His measuring instrument stood elsewhere, beneath the little dome on the bastion. Bohnenberger had this observatory built in 1814 for a large repeating circle, one of the most advanced angle-measuring instruments of its day. The dome could rotate. The instrument thus occupied a room built specifically for its work on the castle bastion.

After Bohnenberger died in 1831, the small observatory fell into obscurity. Almost two centuries after its construction, Tübingen researcher Alfons Renz rediscovered the original instrument there in 2002. More than a historic building had survived: the almost complete repeating circle remained at its original location.

The state heritage authority restored the equipment, while the observatory itself was renovated. The Reichenbach repeating circle returned in 2018, for the two-hundredth anniversary of the start of Württemberg’s survey.

The work undertaken here extended well beyond the castle hill. Bohnenberger’s commission concerned the entire kingdom. The small dome on the bastion and the reference point on the tower belonged to that shared undertaking.

factCards.title: Schlosslabor: DNA from used bandages
factCards.short_description: In the Schlosslabor at Hohentübingen, Friedrich Miescher discovered the substance we now call DNA in 1869. His starting material was used wound dressings from Tübingen’s hospital. He extracted white blood cells from the pus and examined their nuclei, naming the unfamiliar substance nuclein. He did not yet know its role in heredity. His teacher Felix Hoppe-Seyler checked the findings himself before they were published in 1871. The discovery thus began in a converted castle kitchen, with unappealing material and careful verification rather than immediate certainty.
factCards.deep_dive_text:
At the Schlosslabor in Hohentübingen, Friedrich Miescher began studying white blood cells in autumn 1868. The university had converted the former castle kitchen into a chemical laboratory in 1818. Researchers here investigated chemical processes in living organisms. Felix Hoppe-Seyler, appointed professor in Tübingen in 1861, studied the red pigment in blood and named it haemoglobin.

Miescher needed many cells for his experiments. He collected used wound dressings from the hospital and washed white blood cells out of the pus. Early in 1869, he found a previously unknown substance in the cell nuclei. He called it nuclein, after the Latin word for nucleus. To examine it more closely, he used pepsin extracted from pigs’ stomachs. The enzyme broke down proteins, allowing the nuclear substance to be isolated.

Analysis revealed a high phosphorus content. Miescher did not know that the substance carried hereditary information. His teacher did not simply accept the result either: Hoppe-Seyler checked the experiments. Miescher’s work was not published until 1871.

An original preparation made by Miescher survives in the museum. It probably dates from around 1871, when he continued his research in Basel using Rhine salmon. Its label reads “Nuclein aus Lachssperma / F. Miescher”, meaning nuclein from salmon sperm. He had changed his starting material. The small vessel belongs to the continuation of work that began in Tübingen with used bandages.

factCards.title: Kornhaus: grain trading becomes city history
factCards.short_description: The Kornhaus has housed Tübingen’s city museum since 1991, but it was built for very different purposes. Grain was stored and traded below, while townspeople gathered for social occasions upstairs. Schoolchildren later used the building, followed by the fire brigade and Red Cross. Today, the museum also explores Lotte Reiniger’s work. The animation pioneer made films using cut-paper silhouettes from the 1920s onwards. The former commercial building and her delicate film technique tell history at different scales: through the uses of a civic building and through an individual’s creative work.
factCards.deep_dive_text:
The Stadtmuseum occupies the Kornhaus, a building that served the town in several ways over many centuries. Its western part was built in 1453, with the eastern part following about fifty years later. An earlier building on the site had been destroyed by a town fire. The Kornhaus is one of Tübingen’s old utilitarian buildings in the Alemannic timber-framing tradition.

Grain was traded on the lower floor. By the seventeenth century, the upper rooms were used for dancing and social gatherings. Visiting actors also performed plays here. An extra storey had been added in 1604.

A primary school occupied the building in the nineteenth century, teaching children of winegrowers and craftspeople from the lower town. From 1892, the fire brigade and Red Cross used the Kornhaus. Between 1985 and 1991, it was converted into the city museum.

An exhibition about Lotte Reiniger explores the animation pioneer’s silhouette films, which she began making in the 1920s. Her figures involve a very different craft from the building’s timber frame, but both direct attention to constructed forms. Alongside artistic subjects, the museum addresses city history and contemporary questions. The Kornhaus’s own changing uses provide a useful starting point: grain market, meeting place, school and museum occupied the same rooms in succession.
